Constraint Handling Rules is a logic programming language that uses constraints to narrow down search space. It's a powerful tool that expands with the number of atoms in its underlying structure. We've developed a language extension for CHR that enables the representation of more complex data formats, including trees, graphs, and lists, by utilizing recursive constraints and a control mechanism for recursion. We've also introduced a recursive constraint solver and a way to handle inductive definitions. We've evaluated the extension through real-world examples, such as web search algorithms, and found that they showcase a rise in the language's expressive capabilities.

We have analyzed the orientation of galaxies' spin in the SDSS-DR7, 2M++ and the UZCS surveys, and we have compared the results to the large-scale distribution of galaxies and found that the direction of galaxies' spin in each survey aligns with previous research. Our analysis also shows that the direction of galaxies' spin in each survey is consistent with previous findings, and the orientation of galaxies' spin in each survey does not differ significantly from the large-scale structure of the universe. Our analysis also shows that the direction of galaxies' spin in the UZCS survey is consistent with previous findings, and the orientation of galaxies' spin in the UZCS survey aligns with previous research. Our results also show that the direction of galaxies' spin in the UZCS survey aligns with previous research, and the UZCS survey's orientation is not different than the large-scale structure of the universe. Our results also show that the direction of galaxies' spin in the SDSS-DR7 and 2M++ surveys aligns with previous findings, and the direction of galaxies' spin in the SDSS-DR7 and 2M++ surveys aligns with previous research.

We introduce a method called Eigen-Reptile that enables self-supervised learning to tackle the challenges posed by few-shot learning. By adapting the standard self-supervised learning objective to a self-supervised few-shot learning setting, we demonstrate that existing issues with model size, dataset quality, and label noise hinder its effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose a technique that simplifies the representation space through PCA, thereby reducing the parameter count and mitigating the impact of label noise. We also develop a new objective that promotes self-supervised representation learning by focusing on predicting past examples. We validate the efficacy of Eigen-Reptile by achieving state-of-the-art results on well-known few-shot learning benchmarks, while evaluating its robustness to varying levels of label noise.

A novel method for detecting Alzheimer's disease (AD) earlier relies on the analysis of a patient's brain fMRI data while they rest. This method involves the use of a sophisticated neural network that can predict the patient's cognitive status. Past studies have found that patients with AD exhibit distinct brain activity, even while at rest. This study investigates whether the neural network can accurately detect AD from fMRI data, even without prior knowledge of a patient's history. We trained the network using data from 93 AD patients and 76 healthy controls, and it showed a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing between the two groups. Furthermore, the network was able to classify new data from the Amnestic subtype of AD with a 95% accuracy rate. This method has the potential to identify AD earlier and may even detect it before patients show significant cognitive decline, according to previous findings.

This paper proposes an innovative ethical analysis method that can be seamlessly integrated into the AI design process with minimal disruption, while also suggesting a comprehensive framework to enhance ethics education related to AI systems. Our approach synthesizes existing literature in AI ethics, ethics instruction, and cognitive science to develop a pedagogical tool that builds on established concepts. We draw on research in automatic emotion recognition, decision-making, and design to illustrate the practical application of our method. We also outline future research directions that expand beyond the proposed ethical analysis method and and ethics education framework.

We investigate the definability of the full bisimulation relation, denoted F, between ω-words, and consider its reachability and coverability. An ω-word B is said to be reachable from A if there exists another ω-word X, such that the composition of F and X equals A. An ω-word B is coverable from A if there exists a prefix word Y, such that the extension of B by Y equals A. Our research reveals that the definability of reachability and coverability, denoted Fr and Fc, respectively, is not independent, and they are not definable as Boolean combinations of first-order logic predicates. Moreover, we demonstrate that the definability of the bisimulation relation, denoted FF, is not independent from the definability of reachability. It is shown that the definability of reachability and coverability, denoted Fr and Fc, respectively, is unique among decidable Boolean-closed full trios.

A proposed hybrid estimation scheme combines deep neural networks (DNNs) and pilot-aided least-square (LS) estimation techniques for frequency-hopping narrowband wireless channels. By using a DNN to predict the channel response from a reference point in a previous time frame, and then refining those predictions using pilot-aided LS estimation, the scheme significantly reduces the pilot overhead required for accurate channel estimation. Results from simulations show that the proposed method achieves improved accuracy at a lower pilot overhead compared to traditional pilot-aided LS estimation, and nearly achieves the same accuracy with almost no additional pilot overhead when the DNN is trained on data from the specific channel being estimated.

Recent discrepancies in the measurements of V_{ud} and V_{us} appear to be indicating new physics.  A new, heavy vector boson, which would not be part of the Standard Model, could be responsible for the anomalies observed in V_{ud} and V_{us}.  The new vector boson would have to be coupled with quarks.  The implications of this new physics on the measurements of V_{ud} and V_{us}} would be similar to those observed in the neutrino sector.  The new vector boson would be within the reach of current and future neutrino experiments.  The proposed new physics would also affect the measurements of V_{us} due to the presence of a neutral scalar particle, which would also impact measurements of K and D meson decays.

We present an enhanced convolutional neural network, referred to as the Advanced Convolutional Neural Network (ACNN), specifically tailored to tackle the challenging ImageNet classification task, as well as various road scene analysis tasks. By integrating dilated kernels within convolutional layers, our proposed network architecture enables efficient processing of large input images. We investigate the influence of multiple input modalities, including images, LiDAR point clouds, and vehicle tracking data, on the network's performance. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that the ACNN exhibits a significant reduction in computational requirements, achieved through a combination of dilated kernels and a reduced number of network layers, leading to improved efficiency without compromising accuracy.

We propose a novel, language-agnostic method for encoding sensitive information within complex, multi-dimensional datasets. This approach leverages differential privacy to ensure that individual data points cannot be linked to specific attributes. By isolating private details from publicly available ones, we effectively create a framework where an organization can share a dataset while protecting sensitive personal data. To illustrate the practicality of our solution, we demonstrate how it can be integrated with a patient data repository, such as an electronic health record, to enable secure, machine-learning-driven information management systems.

Using the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer data, a comprehensive analysis was conducted to investigate the relationship between hot dust emission from active galactic nuclei and host galaxies. The analysis involved cross-matching WISE data with the International AGN Observing Campaign's catalog, which contains AGN hosts. The results showed a significant correlation between hot dust emission and both the brightness of radio signals and the structure of galaxies. Furthermore, a significant portion of galaxies without visible signs of dust emission produced a measurable hot dust signal. The analysis also found that the mass of supermassive black holes in galaxies positively correlated with the mass of the black holes themselves, but not with the mass of the bulge portion. The findings suggest that the primary cause of hot dust emission is likely dust formed as a result of the accretion process onto black holes, which is then distributed throughout the galaxy. The distribution of dust in these galaxies is consistent with the distribution of stars in these galaxies. The analysis also found that the WISE data can be used to estimate the mass of supermassive black holes in these galaxies.

Recent breakthroughs in language models have enabled them to surpass human performance in many tasks, but they lack the ability to comprehend human thought processes and moral principles. To address this limitation, we developed MORALCOT, an innovative prompting technique, along with a comprehensive dataset called MORAL-LM. Our dataset consists of 4,202 cases from 82 different moral dilemmas, along with 10 natural language sentences representing various arguments that people use to justify their moral choices. Using this dataset, we trained a language model and demonstrated its superior performance in identifying arguments made by both men and women. Our MORALCOT tool is a significant advancement in moral reasoning with language models, allowing AI systems to better understand and analyze human thought processes.

We show that a valuation ring $R$ with a residue field $\kappa$ of positive characteristic $p$ can be represented as the direct limit of a system of $p$-modular algebras. This result implies that $R$ is desingular in the sense that its special fiber is a set of height 1 algebras. We also demonstrate that if the residue characteristic is sufficiently large, then $\operatorname{Spec}^p_R$ is homeomorphic to the classical spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}_p R$.

The two-dimensional Dirac equation equations form a crucial component in the development of quantum electrodynamics and QCD from the underlying principles of quantum field theory, and its comprehensive solution is essential for understanding the behavior of massless fermions in three-dimensional space-time and also in two-dimensional space. This comprehensive solution is crucial for understanding the behavior of massless fermions in three-dimensional space and two-dimensional space. The article will provide an overview of the Dirac equation's two-dimensional solution and its various applications in theoretical physics, including graphene physics and quantum computing. Several methods have been proposed to solve the Dirac equation in two dimensions, and we will explore the potential of using deep learning to discover these solutions.

In cooperative driving settings, the integration of control systems can significantly enhance performance. By leveraging predictions from both environmental models and the intentions of fellow drivers, control outcomes can be optimized. This research introduces a novel control approach, tailored for multi-agent environments, that combines environmental modeling with future intentions. Building on the foundation of Model Predictive Control, the contributions are two-fold: first, a generalized multi-agent formulation of MPC is developed, and second, environmental forecasts and fellow agents' intentions are integrated into the predictive model. The outcomes of this innovative control algorithm are evaluated through both numerical and simulated analyses.

The widespread use of social media has given rise to new concerns regarding information credibility. On one hand, social media can diminish the credibility of established media outlets such as newspapers and television networks. On the other hand, social media platforms present an opportunity for online users to share their personal experiences, providing firsthand knowledge about previously overlooked topics. Notably, social media users' influence on others and their social interactions within online networks can distort the credibility of information. This article aims to explore the relationship between social interactions and information credibility in social networks, with a focus on how to measure the former and how it impacts the latter. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to quantify social interactions and demonstrate its effectiveness in assessing information credibility through experiments and analyses.

Ensuring the safe and efficient flow of traffic is a critical task for highway management, but it is a labor-intensive process that requires a constant watch by highway operators despite the aid of advanced technology. To alleviate the burden of live monitoring and enhance emergency response capabilities, we have developed the $\pi$-ROAD framework. This innovative system integrates intelligent decision support to help operators manage road resources more effectively in the event of an emergency. $\pi$-ROAD leverages a deep learning-based model to forecast traffic conditions and alert highway operators to potential road hazards in advance, thus enabling them to take proactive measures and deploy necessary resources proactively. To further support highway operators, we have also created a comprehensive emergency management platform based on the results of $\pi$-ROAD, which includes an emergency risk alert system, emergency resource dispatching system, and dynamic traffic signal control function. Our experiments demonstrate that $\pi$-ROAD significantly outperforms traditional approaches by providing early warnings to highway operators in advance of critical road hazards, and our emergency management platform can effectively mitigate the risk of road accidents and reduce congestion during emergency response.

This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the Artificial Potential Fields collision avoidance algorithm, which is widely employed in industrial settings. The revised method aims to minimize the detours caused by the original algorithm, resulting in more efficient path planning for robots operating in real-time. By redefining the repulsive force as a gradient of an energy function, the proposed approach can generate a wide range of detour-free paths, even when subjected to multiple obstacles simultaneously. Furthermore, the method can be integrated seamlessly with existing path planners, such as those utilizing potential fields, to form a unified system. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, the authors have developed a simulation environment and conducted case studies to evaluate its performance in various scenarios.

The urban landscape is undergoing a transformative shift with the rise of autonomous vehicles and artificial intelligence, necessitating a fresh perspective on how cities evolve. Our research explores the potential long-term effects on city design, suggesting that increased autonomy and machine intelligence will fundamentally alter city layouts. By analyzing the evolution of mobility networks in New York City over the past 20 years, we discovered a clear trend toward more efficient travel routes and a reduced need for transfer points. Our findings indicate that cities may simplify their infrastructure, reducing congestion and energy waste, and creating more accessible and equitable transportation systems. However, this transformation may exacerbate existing social inequalities unless cities adopt inclusive and forward-looking strategies, taking into account the potential needs and challenges of all members of their society.

In the context of online caching for disk storage, researchers have explored the use of predictions about the files needed. Studies on prediction-free (fully online) caching and predictive caching have yielded optimal algorithms and lower bounds. However, when predictions are inaccurate, the optimal algorithm differs significantly from the online setting. To address this gap, we investigate online caching under imperfect predictions in a sliding window model and establish tight competitive ratios for caching algorithms based on the square of the prediction error and the cache size, providing the first lower bound for caching with inaccurate predictions. Additionally, we demonstrate that a larger cache results in a worse competitive ratio and establish upper and lower bounds for caching with arbitrary and independent identically distributed predictions.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks, particularly when incorporating Trilateral Attention mechanisms, which enable a network to autonomously determine the number of objects it should focus on during training. Despite the success of existing Trilateral Attention methods, there is limited understanding of how the various pathways within the network contribute to overall performance. This work addresses this knowledge gap by investigating the impact of the different object detection pathways on segmentation accuracy, and identifies the most critical pathways for diverse scenarios. By selectively removing underperforming pathways, the investigation demonstrates that the modified Trilateral Attention model can be reduced in size by up to 50% without compromising its accuracy. This streamlined variant is subsequently evaluated on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA datasets, where it achieves competitive results with existing top-performing models, and outperforms them in certain tasks by leveraging just two object detection pathways.

The supergeometry of superspace with torsion has been explored in both a simplified space-time with no torsion and in a modified version with a specific type of torsion that includes a twist.  The torsion in this version of the superspace is essentially a twist that combines gravity and a U(1) gauge field, and this relationship is analogous to a specific mathematical relationship that connects a specific type of derivative to a specific mathematical operator.  This connection allows the torsion constraints to be expressed as a condition on the gauge field itself.  The existence of these torsion constraints implies that the supersymmetry transformations must satisfy a modified version of the Jacobi identity, and this version of the identity involves the commutator of the supersymmetry transformations with each other.

The quality of training data is a significant concern in machine learning, yet pinpointing subpar examples has proven to be a challenging and time-consuming process. Our research presents a novel method to efficiently determine a training example's impact on a model's performance by using the distance between their predictions. This approach was tested across various classification algorithms and comparison methods to evaluate the efficacy of our approach. Our experiments demonstrated that our approach effectively identifies high-quality and potentially problematic examples, and qualitative analyses showed that our results accurately reflect their respective comparison methods. Our work lays the groundwork for further investigation into data comparison methods and highlights the broader application of our example contribution metric.

In a recently proposed model of quantum thermal transport, where a thermal Hall insulator with surface states is subjected to a temperature gradient, two Hall surface states interact through an exchange of phonons. This interaction leads to an interplay between two types of quantum pumping - one related to an abelian matrix Berry phase and the other resulting from a non-abelian matrix Berry phase. This latter effect gives rise to an anomalous pumping of surface Hall states. Crucially, the non-abelian pumping can be controlled by adjusting the temperature gradient and the phonon scattering rate. Furthermore, the anomalous thermal Hall effect can be measured by tracking the quantum charge pumped onto the surface Hall states.

We present METRO-LM, which achieves remarkable efficiency without sacrificing performance, and outperforms previous large models. By combining model compression, transfer learning, and meta-learning techniques, we created a highly efficient and accurate LM. The approach involves pre-training a compact model, transferring it to a larger capacity model, and fine-tuning it. This results in a highly efficient and accurate LM that can be trained in a short period of 1.5 hours on a high-performance server. When deployed on a GPU, it can process 100 billion parameters in real-time. The efficiency of METRO-LM enables it to surpass other models in performance benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art results on common natural language tasks. Additionally, our study provides new insights into the effectiveness of transfer learning and meta-learning for accelerating LM training in various semantic tasks.

We investigate the challenge of reconstructing a quantum network's structure from local measurement data. Conventional methods rely heavily on global connections between all nodes, but our approach is more practical as it focuses on local information. This topology inference problem is relevant to various applications including distributed quantum computing, quantum communication, temperature regulation, and quantum sensing. We demonstrate the potential for developing efficient algorithms using a low-degree polynomial interpolation technique to recover the network's structure from local measurement data. This technique has the advantage of being highly parallelizable, which is crucial for large-scale implementations. We also present two alternative algorithms that utilize uncorrelated random vectors and multivariate polynomials. Furthermore, we analyze the resilience of our algorithms against noise in the local measurements.

A commonly used approach for explaining visual encodings is to employ a step-by-step strategy, yet a recent study suggests this method may not be the most effective way to convey the concept to a general audience who lack technical knowledge.
To address this, researchers designed a novel introduction strategy known as 'Show and Tell', which utilizes a narrative-driven approach to help readers understand the purpose and application of encodings.
This new strategy is comprised of a self-explanatory title, an engaging story, and visual aids illustrating the connection between the title and high-level insights.
The study involved testing the introduction strategy through the creation of 12 interactive web pages, which were evaluated by 28 participants through think-aloud protocols and a 30-day online survey.
The results revealed that readers found the 'Show and Tell' strategy more engaging than the traditional step-by-step strategy, and considered it more effective in conveying the concept of visual encodings.
Furthermore, this strategy also increased readers' intentions to use visual encodings in their own work, indicating its potential to promote wider understanding and adoption of the technology.

We investigate how heating from a driven quantum system affects order in highly interconnected many-body systems, specifically in the context of the transverse field Ising model. We find that an increase in heating is accompanied by a decrease in order, but the type of order that is lost depends on whether the system is being cooled or heated. This understanding provides a framework for managing heating in order to regulate quantum behavior, particularly in large-scale quantum systems.

We investigate the impact of uncertainty in model parameters on the reliability of 
counterfactual plans when the underlying model is unknown. To address this issue, 
we analyze the decision-making process as a problem-solving approach and develop 
a solution based on the combination of sampling and approximation techniques. 
Specifically, we introduce a novel algorithm that employs Monte Carlo sampling to 
create a set of robust counterfactual plans by considering the effects of parameter 
variations on the decision-making process. Theoretical evidence demonstrates the 
efficiency of this method, and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets 
confirm its superiority over existing methods in terms of accuracy in a variety of 
scenarios.

This paper presents an efficient deep learning model that uses a convolutional network to identify sounds in images. The model consists of a single path with three convolutional layers and can be trained on a specific device before being run on another device. The model was specifically designed to classify urban sounds by converting audio into visual data and processing it for better results. The proposed model achieved higher accuracy compared to similar systems on the ESC-50 and US8k datasets, reaching 60.45% and 64.89% top-1 accuracy respectively. The model's performance was also evaluated for on-board audio classification systems.

We explore solutions within $AdS_2\times S^2$ and $AdS_2\times H^2$ space with specific parameters that correspond to $AdS_4$ black holes in a four-dimensional, gravitating, supersymmetric theory. These solutions are derived from a specific state in a supersymmetric theory where the field's non-zero value is protected by a principle, resulting in a specific pattern of how fields interact with each other.

The Code Optimisation Benchmark for Astronomy (Coba) is a program designed to evaluate and compare the efficiency of different compilers by running a set of astronomical algorithms through various compilers and assessing their performance. In this paper, we investigate the potential of Cain, a compiler based on the C++-like Language, to process the SCAMP-5 test suite, focusing on the generated code's characteristics. The results indicate that the code produced by any other compiler is 0.9 to 12% longer than that generated by Cain, which suggests a relatively minor improvement. Furthermore, our findings show that the execution time of the code produced by Cain is comparable to or even slightly faster than that of the code produced by other compilers in all cases.

We investigate the Witten effect within the context of the holographic duality in AdS/CFT, specifically focusing on how it relates to the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity. Our research reveals that the generalized Witten effect is indeed a characteristic feature of the Dirac sea, but its application is restricted in cases where the chemical potential is insufficient to access the entire Dirac sea. As a result, the Witten effect's behavior is highly dependent on the quantum vacuum from which charged particles originate.

In this research, we investigate the efficacy of regret pruning, a technique developed by Perkins et al., 2020, for learning Nash equilibria. Two pruned variants are presented to address the drawbacks of the original method. A regression-based implementation demonstrates the effectiveness of these variations in a simulated environment. A regression-based approach outperforms its original non-regret pruning counterpart in learning Nash equilibria while maintaining data efficiency. These advancements are further utilized to develop a new algorithm, termed RPR, for learning Nash equilibria in non-stationary settings. RPR's capacity to adapt to changing environments is showcased through a case study involving a 3x3 Zero-Sum Games network where two players can move to adjacent cells.

This article introduces a novel modal logic designed to reevaluate and expand Aristotle's modal syllogistic by conceptualizing possible states-of-affairs. Key features of this framework are demonstrated through its ability to explain and validate Aristotle's modal syllogistic, particularly those that earlier systems have struggled to account for. The approach also offers a clear and rigorous formal structure, enabling the derivation of modal axioms linked to modality. The resulting system is shown to be both sound and complete, setting the stage for a comprehensive modal logic system.

In quantum mechanics, Bell-type inequalities assess correlations between measurement results, yet these correlations can disappear when particle pairs are separated by space and time. While quantum mechanics predicts this phenomenon, a surprising finding emerges: in a specific class of inequalities, a certain level of measurement efficiency is not sufficient for correlations to vanish. This contrasts sharply with classical models, where correlations persist regardless of measurement efficiency. This novel class of causal inequalities necessitates reevaluating traditional notions of physical causation and separation.

This study introduces a dual-critic reinforcement learning framework for the video rate-distortion mean squared error (MSE) optimization problem. Unlike existing methods that optimize a single objective function, our approach leverages two critics to simultaneously control distortion and rate, enabling more precise regulation of their trade-off. The proposed framework relies on a deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) to learn the policy parameters. In experiments, our method demonstrated superior performance over conventional and learning-based state-of-the-art solutions, yielding 10-15% better PSNR results. The implementation details, including code and models, are accessible on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/xiangying2018/DRCL.

The intricate dynamics of protoplanetary disk chemistry is a result of a delicate balance between chemical reactions in the gas and a steady supply of elements from carbon-rich particles that have been broken down through exposure to ultraviolet light. We have developed a comprehensive model that simulates the photo-ablative destruction of carbon-rich planetary particles and their subsequent contribution to the chemical reactions in the disk. Our findings indicate that the photo-ablative destruction of carbon-rich particles can sustain a stable chemical cycle in the disk for an extended period, as long as the surface density of carbon-rich particles exceeds a certain threshold. Conversely, if this threshold is not met, the chemical cycle collapses irreversibly. We discovered that maintaining the stable chemical cycle is contingent upon factors such as the UV radiation field, the destruction cross-section, and the photo-ablative efficiency of the particles. Our model also reveals that the stable chemical cycle can persist for millions of years, producing a consistent pattern of molecular species. We further demonstrate that the stable chemical cycle can be maintained in disks with relatively low levels of UV radiation, provided their surface density of carbon-rich particles exceeds a certain threshold.

In mixed-integer linear programming, selecting a single optimal solution often involves choosing a specific solution from a set of optimal alternatives. A common approach is to use a single heuristic, which may result in suboptimal outcomes for alternative objectives. A novel approach, NeuralCut, employs a neural network to learn the priority of solutions based on multiple objectives and can be integrated seamlessly with existing solvers. Experimental results demonstrate NeuralCut significantly outperforms baseline methods in both exact and infeasible cases, with a 7.9% improvement in test accuracy and 4.2% decrease in solving time.

The study of Mo$_{1-x}$W$_x$Te$_2$ single crystals, a topological superconductor candidate, has led researchers to investigate similar compounds, such as T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_x$Te$_2$, for their unique superconducting properties. These properties, characterized by zero resistance at 2 K and a temperature-dependent resistivity, suggest that T$_d$-Mo$_{1-x}$Ir$_x$Te$_2$ exhibits a magnetic field-induced superconducting state, similar to T$_d$-MoTe$_2$. This compound's behavior is attributed to the presence of a nodal excitation gap, as indicated by the temperature dependence of its resistivity, and is consistent with theories that describe the interplay between a magnetic field and a magnetic material.

Software bug report retrieval has seen significant advancements, driven by research into effective feature and similarity function design. Despite these breakthroughs, the majority of research focuses on similarity functions, leaving the task of extracting relevant attributes underrepresented. We introduce a method to utilize NLP techniques for extracting and ranking feature attributes. Our approach consists of three key components: a named entity recognition model, a dependency parser, and a term matching algorithm. These components enable the conversion of complete bug reports into attribute-level descriptions, ultimately facilitating a more precise similarity assessment between bug reports. We evaluated our approach on a dataset of historical bug reports from the Mozilla project and observed substantial improvements in identical bug report retrieval, outperforming state-of-the-art baseline methods in our experiment.

A strongly coupled effective field theory for graphene's phase transitions near its key features is introduced. This theory incorporates key elements from chiral sigma models, including dynamic boson masses and a four-loop self-energy correction, as well as a unique non-linear connection between Goldstone fields and their couplings. Derived from this model, critical properties of charge density waves in graphene are calculated, providing a theoretical foundation for predicting observable properties, such as the critical temperature and critical exponent, of charge density waves in graphene.

We introduce a teacher-student framework that leverages self-training to enhance NER models. Our key innovation is a new approach to self-training that accurately captures NER's value in providing guidance: by focusing on examples the student can easily process and accurately label, and then using these high-quality labels to refine the student model. Our approach is built upon the observation that the most valuable examples for teachers are those that students can reliably label; in contrast, training on difficult examples results in poor student labels and unhelpful teacher refinement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework across multiple NER models and datasets, and show that it outperforms alternative self-training methods and competitive non-self-training techniques. Our implementation code is freely available on GitHub.

This paper showcases a cutting-edge system for extracting meaningful insights from large social media datasets containing user-generated content and tags related to tourist attractions. By leveraging a vast amount of data collected from the city of Rome's past events, the system employs an innovative text-to-tag-to-text generative model, which learns relationships between text and tags from the input data. Once trained, the system can transform text into tags and generate tags based on given text, ultimately allowing the extraction of valuable information such as popular tourist attractions, visitor demographics, and event attendance. Furthermore, the text-to-tag-to-tag system's output can be refined through a self-supervised pre-training technique that utilizes the model's own generated tags to improve tag assignment accuracy. Our research highlights the potential of the extracted insights for supporting high-level decision-making in the travel and hospitality industry.

To determine the effectiveness of materials with microstructured properties, researchers employ techniques such as finite element methods, which are computationally demanding. This work introduces a novel approach using machine learning to efficiently predict material effectiveness, enabled by a significant new dataset comprising over 250,000 effective material properties. This dataset, accessible through the repository "ML Effective Materials," is also equipped with tools for data analysis and ranking. This dataset has been developed to facilitate the comparison of various machine learning algorithms.

A new study of the CI Tau system from the VLT/SPHERE instrument has found no evidence to support the theory of planetary migration caused by tidal heating from companion CI Tau b. Using a novel imaging technique, researchers were able to estimate an upper limit on the heat emitted by the planet, finding it to be much lower than the estimated required to cause migration. However, this result contradicts previous simulations, and as a result, it has become unlikely that tidal heating from CI Tau b can cause the planet's migration. Additionally, researchers were able to observe the planet in its early stages, finding its surface temperature to be around 700 to 800 Kelvin. This result further contradicts previous simulations, which had suggested that the planet would migrate and warm up rapidly. Furthermore, researchers were able to observe the disk surrounding the star, finding it to be more complex than initially thought. Using a new disk model, researchers were able to estimate the mass of material within the disk at around 1.6 times 10 to the negative 2 power solar masses, with significant scatter. This material is likely to be a remnant of the initial material that surrounded the star at its birth, with a total mass of around 0.08 solar masses.

We demonstrate that in a certain scenario where two potential functions combine, all zero-energy trajectories in the combined potential coincide with finite-energy spherical free motion trajectories when the higher-order potential function is eliminated. Conversely, for a potential where a unique minimum exists at the origin, all zero-energy trajectories in the combined potential intersect as the origin for any non-zero linear momentum, while the lowest energy level, which is non-positive, corresponds uniquely within the interior of the resulting spherical billiard system.

We examine a class of nonlinear equations featuring non-linear operators and perturbations, with certain conditions ensuring the presence of at least one non-trivial solution. These equations are parameterized by real numbers within a given interval, and through a series of precise mathematical arguments, we establish the range of possible parameter values that support such solutions. Our research extends the scope of a previous study in this field, and involves the application of a recent result on the spectral properties of operators, specifically the boundedness and continuity of associated function spaces. Our primary findings are consolidated in a companion note that provides a comprehensive and simplified proof of this key result.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking technique for estimating trajectories in unclassified multi-object filtering contexts. By applying particle filtering to both predicted and measured data, along with corresponding control variables, the method enhances the tracking capabilities of existing algorithms. A key advantage of this approach lies in its ability to utilize predicted information from control inputs, which provides valuable insights into the objects' trajectories. Consequently, the method offers valuable data for tracking and trajectory prediction, especially when applied to autonomous vehicles. Experimental results, conducted using a sophisticated unified multi-object tracking framework on the KITTI dataset, demonstrate the significant improvement achieved through this technique.

This study introduces a new stability assessment criterion, rooted in the control barrier function, for small signal stability analysis. This method enhances the accuracy of equilibrium stability assessments and expands its applicability to critical regions of large power systems with high penetration of power converters. The proposed criterion is validated through numerical tests on a 68-bus system, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying unstable equilibria in systems with significant power converter involvement.

A recent study developed a 56-templates set for a signature recognition system, enabling the evaluation of distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of signatures. However, limited data prevented the exploration of these factors in the same dataset. To address this, researchers utilized a large-scale dataset consisting of 202,049 signatures from 1,652 signers. The data was divided into three sets of 56-signatures, allowing for the examination of signature distinctiveness, complexity, and repeability. The findings indicate that signatures with higher distinctiveness, complexity, and repeability scores exhibit better verification performance.

The standard approach views Hardy sums as a transformation linking almost periodic functions within the real numbers to functions on the unit circle. This paper offers an alternative perspective, translating Hardy sums into a sum of oriented geodesics for a hyperbolic surface and subsequently linking it to the theory of affine modular forms.

The growing adoption of mobile devices is driving the need for innovative solutions to effectively utilize their capabilities.  Mobile applications are becoming increasingly popular for a wide range of tasks, but their potential is limited by the complexity and diversity of user interactions.  To fully leverage the applications' functionality, an adaptive and personalized approach is necessary.  This study examines the use of contextual values as a means of customizing applications to suit individual users.  By utilizing a persistent digital record of users' situations, an informed decision-making process can be developed.  Our research proposes a framework for incorporating contextual values into mobile applications and incorporates it into a game.  Our findings indicate that users' situations have a significant impact on the quality of gaming experience.  Our study also reveals that incorporating contextual values into application design can lead to enhanced user experience and improved performance.  Our results also reveal that providing users with multiple choices for adjusting contextual values can improve overall satisfaction.  Our study contributes to the development of mobile applications that take into account the diversity of situations in which they are used, enabling a more personalized experience.

We present an efficient real-time system for 3D pose estimation from images, where a novel architecture enables a network to solve the task in a streamlined manner, effectively reducing the process into two sequential, more manageable parts: 2D keypoint detection and 2D-to-3D transformation. By limiting the network's complexity, it can perform the keypoint detection quickly, and then use these results to compute the 3D poses without encountering the typical trade-offs between accuracy and speed. This approach allows the network to focus on a specific problem at each stage, and we show that it's capable of delivering real-time performance with high accuracy across various tasks involving human pose prediction.

Between 2017 and 2019, the soft X-ray instrument CMC on board the AstroSat observed a variety of sources, including Comptonization models, X-ray pulsars, a millisecond pulsar, a black hole, and soft X-ray background, in order to calibrate the CMC detector accurately. The results showed that the measurements from AstroSat are reliable and comparable to ground-based observations of the Sun, a millisecond pulsar and an X-ray pulsar, but not as sensitive as other space-based X-ray observatories. The observations of the Sun were also used to determine the short-term variability of the X-ray pulsar 1E 1047.1 by comparing its flux with data from other instruments. The results showed that the AstroSat measurements of 1E 1047.1 were consistent with those from other instruments, even though the other instruments had a higher sensitivity. The observations of the millisecond pulsar SAX J2103.4+4647 also showed a consistent measurement of its spin period accretion. The results also showed that the background observed by the AstroSat matches the expected spectrum of the cosmic X-ray background.

This paper presents a comprehensive examination of the core features of blockchain technology and their inherent characteristics. It delves into the fundamental properties that enable the realization of the technology, including its permission-to-participate model, participation authorization protocol, incentive mechanisms, network architecture, consensus protocols, smart contract specifications, language characteristics, and interoperability between systems. We delve into the distinct attributes of each these properties and provide an in-depth analysis of permissionless and permissioned blockchain protocols, based on the variations in each property. Furthermore, we discuss the unique characteristics of consensus protocols, such as Byzantine Fault Tolerance and finality guarantees, and examine the properties of smart contract languages, such as formality and semantics.

The chromomagnetic interaction model has been enhanced to improve its ability to handle compact tetraquark states, with a focus on modifying the interaction potential between interchanged constituent quarks. This revised model was then applied to calculate the mass spectra of established tetraquark states, specifically the $X(4000)$, $X(4500)$, and $X(5300)$ states, with a new universal coupling parameter also being considered. The results show that mass spectra are more accurately described when considering the improved interaction, with a predicted value for the $X(4000)$ state aligning with its experimental mass within a margin of $35$ MeV. Additionally, the revised model reduces the disparity between predicted and experimental masses for the $X(4500)$ and $X(5300)$ states, with a further investigation into the potential tetraquark nature of these states involving the improved interaction.

We investigate the Standard Model's extension, incorporating a dimension-6 set of operators, which includes a dimensionless parameter beta that measures the scaling of these operators. Focusing on a specific process, Hubble friction is found to be proportional to beta squared. Setting beta to below 10^-13 suffices to ensure that the Higgs mass exceeds 125 GeV. Furthermore, our research indicates that limiting beta below 10^-15 is sufficient to guarantee the stability of cold dark matter comprised of fermionic particles with masses around 10 GeV. Ultimately, our findings suggest that beta must be less than 10^-13 to satisfy both Higgs mass constraints and dark matter stability criteria.

This research delves into the relationships between the Hamilton-Jacobi equation and $p$-Talagrand inequality within the context of Carnot groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that solutions to the $p$-Talagrand inequality are equivalent to the Hamilton-Jacobi equation under a particular condition. Our analysis builds on existing work by Figalli and Sanz-Soler, who established the same connection for $p=1$, which we then generalize for any value of $p$ using specific techniques and new geometric insights.

We've developed a new estimator, the exponentially weighted divergence (EWD) estimator, based on the affinity function $e^{x-y}K(x,y)$. This estimator is a modified version of the density power divergence (DPD) estimator, which is well-established in literature, but suffers from certain limitations. Our research evaluates the performance of EWD and DPD estimators under optimal exponential weights and minimum divergence conditions. The results show that EWD outperforms DPD, with DPD being more susceptible to outliers and exhibiting bias. The estimators' asymptotic properties are compared, with DPD being a biased estimator and EWD not being asymptotically unbiased. The estimators are applied to various data sets, with EWD demonstrating better resistance to outliers compared to DPD.

This study introduces a novel image analysis algorithm designed to automatically
differentiate between pixels that require motion compensation and those that don't.
Building on the concept of video frames being a series of images superimposed with
motion, the proposed algorithm leverages machine learning to pinpoint dynamic image
components. In a data-driven approach, a deep convolutional neural network is trained
on a vast dataset of aligned images, then utilized to predict motion-induced errors
in subsequent frames. In the results section, examples demonstrate how the proposed
algorithm effectively identifies areas of the image that necessitate motion
compensation to achieve precise alignment.

In this study, we investigate how the periodic orbits of a complex hyperbolic circle group influence the coefficients of its characteristic polynomial. It is already understood that the coefficients follow a Bessel function pattern, yet our findings suggest this relationship holds true even when periodic orbits intersect themselves, a phenomenon not previously considered. By utilizing the Iwasawa theorem to decompose the mod p points of G into its periodic components, our research reveals that the variance of the Bessel function is proportional to the number of self-intersections in the periodic orbits.

The Gaia mission has successfully observed periodic variable stars across a wide range of periods and amplitudes, thanks to its precision photometry. We have developed a classification tool that utilizes the HESS4 light curves and categorizes them according to their properties. The technique employs the Hotelling T^2 distance metric and supports vector regression and variable selection. We have successfully applied this method to 1.39 million Gaia variables and identified 1.02 million eclipsing binaries and nebular variables. The latter group encompasses 1.01 million classical eclipsing binaries and 33 thousand NEB variables. We have also validated our tool by comparing it to a simulated dataset and have successfully isolated specific types of variables, such as long-period RS CVn variables and W Uma variables. The tool has also successfully provided estimates of physical properties, such as luminosity and effective temperatures, for various types of variables, thanks to its use of HESS4 data.

This research focuses on a class of linear, time-invariant systems characterized by a non-negative imaginary characteristic matrix, referred to as $\omega$-stable systems. A new, efficient method for determining the nearest $-\omega$-stable system is presented, where the nearest $-\omega$-stable system is defined as the $-\omega$-stable system that minimizes the L2 distance to the original system. This distance is measured by the trace of the product of two matrices: the coupling matrix and the negative conjugate transpose of the original matrix. Notably, the proposed method involves only a polynomial number of computational steps, making it an improvement over the standard semidefinite program approach. Furthermore, the method is applied to solve related optimal disturbance location problems and is demonstrated using a numerical example.

Continuous learning in End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition (E2ESR) poses significant challenges. Presently available solutions for adapting E2ER models to new tasks involve fine-tuning pre-trained models, but this approach can hinder performance on the initial task and requires substantial data for new tasks. We have conducted an evaluation that compares various approaches to continual learning, including fine-tuning as a control group. We discovered that our proposed method, known as the Multitask Progressive Continual Learning algorithm, can improve E2ER model accuracy on new tasks by up to 11.8% relative in the initial training data and reduce the required data for new tasks by up to 50%.

In our study, we introduce an innovative approach to sentiment analysis for social media posts containing code-switched English and Arabic text. To our knowledge, this research is the first to tackle this challenge, which is crucial for enhancing social media automated analysis in mixed language contexts. We provide an in-depth examination of code-switching among bilingual speakers and its implications for sentiment analysis models. Using our dataset of 3,125 manually annotated social media posts from the Middle East, we investigate how various machine learning models, both in English and Arabic, perform on this specific domain. Our results indicate that a multilingual BERT model, trained on four languages, achieves the best sentiment analysis performance for this task.

A three-loop standard model variant incorporating the seesaw mechanism exactly preserves the standard model's interactions in the electroweak symmetry limit, thereby yielding predictions for the lightest right-handed neutrino mass at 129 GeV or below. The minimal standard model variant we are examining features a single complex gauge group scalar in addition to right-handed neutrinos, which are responsible for generating tiny neutrino masses through the three-loop interaction $S
u
u
u$. The minimal model's Yukawa interactions are constrained by a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, which is a defining characteristic of this scenario. The minimal standard model's predictions are compatible with the results of lepton flavor violation experiments, while its predictions for the right-handed neutrino's mixing angle with the standard model's regular neutrinos could potentially be probed in future collider studies.

The increasing availability of categorical data in statistical and machine learning applications has led to a growing interest in the field. Despite the prevalence of categorical data, most deep learning architectures have been designed with continuous inputs in mind. This paper presents a novel deep learning architecture called the Product-based Neural Network (PNN), specifically developed for handling categorical data. By incorporating product-based interactions between categorical fields, the PNN is well-suited for handling complex query and dependency relationships, making it a useful tool in recommender systems. Through empirical evaluation, the PNN has demonstrated superior performance compared to existing deep learning models in various recommendation system tasks.

This paper tackles the complex issue of joint active beamforming and intelligent reflecting surface design in a hybrid downlink network that incorporates an intelligent reflecting surface. To address the challenge, we develop a solution to the beamforming optimization problem by leveraging a reparameterization approach. We introduce a reparameterization model that incorporates uncertainty in channel state information to enable the estimation of the optimal beamforming vector. To solve the optimization problem, we develop a novel multiple Lyapunov variables-based framework, and derive the necessary conditions for optimal solutions and constraints. To solve the reparameterized problem, we develop a semi-definite programming formulation and propose a solution using a semi-definite relaxation. To address the CSI uncertainty, we develop a method to estimate the CSI covariance matrix using a Monte Carlo simulation algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms benchmark algorithms in terms of energy efficiency, while satisfying constraints.

This study delves into the predictive performance of a static branch predictor and two dynamic predictors, employing both static and deep learning-based approaches. Results indicate that static prediction generally outperforms deep learning-based dynamic prediction in 5 consecutive instances of the SPEC benchmarks. A proposed hybrid predictor, combining static and static-ML predictions, is also presented. This hybrid predictor balances predictive accuracy and the cost of training deep learning models, as it eliminates the need for model retraining with each new benchmark.

This research paper presents a camera control system utilizing a deep convolutional neural network to monitor and analyze video feed in real-time. Leveraging the capabilities of a deep learning model, our system enables efficient video processing, allowing for rapid identification of target features, tracking, and the ability to manipulate camera parameters without prior knowledge of image resolution. By integrating a neural network for video processing and a control mechanism operating on a frame-by-frame basis, we have developed a flexible system for optimizing camera settings and responding to target changes. To demonstrate its performance, we have tested our system on various targets, including known and unknown features, comparing it favorably with state-of-the-art techniques.

We conducted a thorough SOS analysis using the auxiliary basin principle to find boundary laws in the SOS model. The principle helped us discover boundary laws that couldn't be normalized, along with those with zero boundary probability in specific cases. Additionally, by representing the model as a specific type of random walk, we examined their properties and found that one non-normalisable boundary law effectively acts as a trap for the model. This analysis also enabled us to identify a connection between the model and a well-known growth process called the TASEP, resulting in further insights into the behavior of the boundary boundary laws.

Theoretical models of resonant energy transfer have typically assumed a direct link between the energy donor and acceptor, but this paper demonstrates that entangled photons can create an effective interaction that allows for energy transfer through non-linear interactions. The effective rate constant governing this entangled transfer can be determined using the dynamics of the interacting particles and their relative position. The predicted rates show that while entangled transfer rates are generally smaller than their classical counterparts, they depend on the overlap of the energy levels of the interacting particles and do not decrease with distance.

We use the light-cone approach to construct the parton distribution functions
of the pion and our results are compared to those obtained through other
methods. We then employ these sum rules to calculate the strong coupling
constants, which align with other approaches within expected error margins.
Additionally, we use the same sum rules to determine the pion distribution
amplitude slope, where our results are consistent with existing experimental
findings within error tolerances.

Recent neutrino experiment data has revealed intriguing anomalies that align with predictions from certain short-baseline experiments, which warrant more comprehensive investigation. We investigate the potential of a large-scale experiment situated within the Near Detector pool at the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility to thoroughly explore the parameter space related to these anomalies. Our analysis indicates that by focusing on specific neutrino beams and comparing measurements with baseline expectations, a large-scale experiment can effectively identify or disprove relevant oscillation mechanisms. Ultimately, the experiment's design suggests significant potential for the near-term neutrino community to contribute significantly to resolving the observed anomalies.

A straightforward statistical approach can be used to determine weights that correlate with treatment assignment, which in turn enables the design of observational studies for drawing causal conclusions. However, this strategy relies on regression methods that may produce unreliable results when data is scarce. To address this challenge, we have developed efficient techniques to identify and correct errors caused by insufficient data. Our new methods not only streamline the process of identifying and refining weights for smaller datasets, as well as their corresponding outcomes. Furthermore, they can be integrated into existing software packages without necessitating programming. Our results from both simulated and genuine studies confirm the efficacy of these approaches.

This paper outlines a novel control strategy for synchronously and asynchronously powered voltage source converters (VSCs) to damp oscillations stemming from grid disturbances at very high frequencies. The introduced control method is an extension of the well-established local damping factor (LDF) method, which has been widely used to damp low-frequency oscillations. The proposed strategy utilizes the extended phase lead of power systems and control VSCs at high frequencies to damp out local disturbances. The method is applied to both synchronous and asynchronous grids, with the introduction of a new method to determine the damping factor for asynchronous powered VSCs. The proposed strategy is tested using a simulation model of the French-German power grid, which is modified to include high-frequency lines, with the results of the tests presented through simulation diagrams and mathematical data.

We investigate the evolution of a tripartite quantum system consisting of two atoms and a noninertial observer, focusing on the Schwinger and Hartle models. These observers, moving with the Earth and a high-speed cosmic body, interact with the vacuum field, causing the creation of a particle-antiparticle pair. We analyze how these primordial particles evolve over time within a multi-level atom with internal structure, and calculate the emission spectrum of the atom's transition to its ground state. Our results show that the atom's transition to its ground state from an excited state through two channels of internal transitions leads to the emission of photons with a tendency to exhibit EPR-correlations, thus producing entangled photons with opposite momentum directions.

The impact of internal modes on kink stability is investigated within the context of the $\varphi^4$ model, where a long-lived metastable solution supports kinks. When lower-energy states become accessible, kinks can potentially decay through mode mixing. However, our analysis shows that the interaction between an unstable kink and an $O(3)$ kink type is actually stabilizing due to increased potential energy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the largest eigenvalue associated with this process tends towards a negative value as the kink's lifetime comes to an end. Moreover, we have found that the rate of kink decay is influenced by the specific initial conditions chosen for the simulation.

We investigate the connection between generalized parton distributions and hadron production, focusing on the specific case of Drell-Yan processes. Our research aims to provide a comprehensive framework for linking GPDs to experimental data in a comprehensive way. Furthermore, we derive formulas that relate GPDs to observables in exclusive exclusive experiments, such as hadronic tensor components and longitudinal beam spin asymmetries. Our approach is demonstrated through an in-depth analysis of a Drell-Yan experiment at the HERA collider, which we use to estimate the uncertainty associated with the extracted GPDs. Our results show that the GPDs F, H, and E can be accurately determined from the longitudinal beam spin asymmetry and the transverse asymmetry of the Drell-Yan process.

The integration of neural language models with non-neural NLP techniques has led to a surge in research across various NLP tasks. In this study, we focus on combining neural language models with discrete noise in text classification to enhance performance. By adding discrete noise to the training model's decision boundary, our approach can influence the neural network's output distribution, thereby optimizing classification head loss during training. Our method, dubbed Perturbed Decision Boundary Optimization (PDBO), is a real-time process occurring within training sessions. We successfully applied PDBO to a range of tasks, utilizing the Adam optimizer for comparison purposes. Our results demonstrate that PDBO can improve state-of-the-art performance by 1.5% or more across 8 out of 10 NLP tasks, including a significant 3.4% increase on the AGNEWS dataset. Our code is available for public access on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jamesbob123/PDBO.

To efficiently extract relevant features from video data, traditional convolutional neural networks rely on overlapping operations.  However, in the context of computer-assisted polyp detection from endoscopic procedures, the need to examine each frame in detail is crucial due to the high resolution of the endoscope.  Consequently, the overlapping operation significantly increases the computational cost.  A novel approach, the channel-aware attention (CA-attention) technique, is introduced to address this challenge.  By applying a channel-wise attention block to feature embeddings, CA-attention enables the optimal aggregation of features from multiple frames.  The proposed method introduces a CA-attention module to the feature extraction stage of the Deep Learning U-net, and its performance is evaluated on the Kvasir-SEG dataset.  The results demonstrate that the CA-Net model, which incorporates CA-attention, achieves a higher detection score, and its dice score is significantly higher than the baseline model.

We've developed an improved sequential sampling approach, where we select a
random subset of candidates for further evaluation in each round of evaluation.
The candidates in each round are chosen based on a predetermined minimum
number of distinct features, ensuring that our sampling method maintains a
desirable level of overall spread. The spread of the chosen candidates can be
adjusted by increasing or decreasing the required number of distinct features.
To ensure that the chosen candidates are maximally diverse, we employ a
specific algorithm that iteratively selects candidates from the top of the
list until a predetermined number of chosen candidates with the desired level
of diversity are identified.

Type-I X-ray bursts originate from rapid neutron capture processes occurring during brief X-ray bursts when material outside a neutron star's surface undergoes intense nuclear reactions.  Although researchers have made significant progress in understanding these burst nucleosynthesis processes through both theoretical models and observations, there is still a gap in knowledge about how certain crucial nuclear reactions, particularly those involving proton-rich nuclei, proceed.  Specifically, researchers have been trying to determine the extent to which certain nuclear reactions, particularly those involving nickel-56, play a role in producing certain heavy elements, but this question has been difficult to answer due to limitations in computational power and the complexity of the problem.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a new computational model that simulates these burst nucleosynthesis processes by combining advanced algorithms with high-performance computing capabilities.  By using this model to analyze both simulated and observed X-ray burst events, researchers have been able to determine the extent to which certain nuclear reactions, particularly those involving nickel-56 and other heavy elements, contribute to producing certain rare isotopes, including those with atomic numbers greater than 78.  Their findings suggest that while certain nuclear reactions, particularly those involving nickel-56, play a significant role in producing certain rare isotopes, other reactions, particularly those involving smaller nuclei, may also be playing a role in producing these rare elements, but more research is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

We examine the structure of the connected components comprising torsion classes in abelian schemes, particularly those identified in the zero group scheme. By extension, our work extends to investigating the analogous structure within principal polarized moduli spaces, specifically examining the components of the zero subvariety. By employing a specific morphism that maps abelian schemes to principal polarized moduli spaces, we establish a correspondence between the connected components of zero subvarieties across different cases, namely abelian varieties and certain types of curves.

A decade ago, The Very High Energy Gamma-Ray Telescopes detected their first galactic source of Gamma Rays, which marked a significant shift from focusing on extragalactic sources, and since then there has been a drastic change in our understanding of Gamma Ray emission at Galactic scales. In this article, we will discuss the recent advancements in Very High Energy Gamma Ray observations from galactic sources and highlight the role of the Major Atmospheric Imaging Cherenkov Telescope (MAGIC). The capabilities and upgrades of the next-generation MAGIC will also be discussed.

This research delves into nonlocal boundary-distributed in time problems, examining how the dynamics of diffusion change as their nonlocal characteristics shift in a spatially confined environment that mimics real-world physical obstacles, while also uncovering topological features of the resulting solutions. By applying nonlocal two-sided Laplace operators, we investigate the resulting systems of ordinary differential equations and identify the impact of boundary conditions on the solutions' behavior, ultimately uncovering distinct topological characteristics of the phase space. Additionally, we derive and analyze an explicit and smooth solution to the problem, using an explicit formula that can be applied to any closed or open domain, as well as any given function. Finally, we illustrate our findings with numerical examples, providing concrete evidence to support our analysis.

Determining the nature of mysterious compact stellar systems in nearby galaxies is a key issue in modern astrophysics, with numerous enigmatic objects discovered recently. To create a novel classifier capable of identifying these systems, we designed a deep learning framework based on a U-Net model, which incorporates a fully convolutional architecture. We utilized the LSST's color imaging data and pre-trained the model using a dataset of 1000 stellar objects. We then tested the model with 1000 new objects and found that it can accurately classify compact stellar objects. Our analysis revealed that $g-r$ and $r-i$ colors are the most informative for classification, followed by $u-r$ color. Furthermore, we found that our model's performance is influenced by stellar color and luminosity. Our results also indicate that our model can accurately classify objects in simulated $uBVr-SSP$ color spaces. We provide an open-source Python package, PyCompStellar, which enables researchers to analyze and classify compact stellar systems in nearby galaxies using the $g-r$ and $r-i$ colors. Our model's code and data are available for public access on GitHub, allowing researchers to adapt and apply the model to various datasets.

Recommender Systems play a vital role in our daily lives, influencing numerous decisions people make. However, the process of designing and maintaining these systems is complex and labor-intensive.  To streamline this process, researchers have explored using simulations to evaluate different strategies and systems.  This paper aims to provide an overview of simulation methods for recommender systems, serving as a reference for those interested in this field. It offers a comprehensive survey of simulation tools, techniques, and applications, serving as a guide for practitioners.

This paper addresses a hypothesis test for distributions that have either infinite means or unbounded variances by utilizing the characteristics of truncated sample means. It shows that by analyzing the limiting behavior of a particular ratio, derived from sample-based estimates, which approach defined values at rates influenced by the distribution characteristics, our hypothesis can be determined. Additionally, we investigate the distribution of the ratio's test statistic under the null hypothesis, providing a basis for determining critical bounds. Our approach is particularly applicable when the alternative distribution shares the same one-sided support as the null distribution. In this context, we demonstrate that our hypothesis test achieves consistency and uniform asymptotically exact level of significance. We also establish the importance of our results by showing that hypothesis testing based on sample means is either inconsistent or fails to achieve asymptotic significance in a finite number of trials, unless the null and alternative distributions are identical. Our findings are further supported through a simulation study.

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) have significant potential to assist individuals with paralysis caused by disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Currently, most high-performing BCIs utilize electroencephalography (EEG) for user input. The primary feature of EEG signals in BCIs are time-dependent, and they are typically processed using time-focused techniques like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to achieve accurate classification. Nevertheless, these methods often require substantial data, memory, and processing power, which can hinder their practical application. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative framework that extracts and stores the crucial features of EEG signals during the training process. This approach significantly reduces the memory and data needed for classification, and it is suitable for implementation on various intelligent devices, such as those designed for wearable applications. Through extensive experiments on two distinct datasets, we have demonstrated the efficacy of our method in facilitating motor-imagery BCIs, and we have shown that it is capable of achieving performance comparable to the current state-of-the-art while minimizing memory and data requirements. The associated code and models are freely available for download at https://github.com/brainlabai/BCI.

The research investigates noncommutative BMS4 x S2 superalgebras in massive scalar fields within the AdS/CFT framework, specifically using the local coordinate-free definition of noncommutative spacetime as described in the arXiv:09010.0625 paper. This approach focuses on the noncommutative superalgebra's symmetry properties and develops a corresponding covariant action for the scalar field, then identifies conserved charges associated with the algebra's generators. These charges are calculated using Noether's theorem and associated with superalgebra's symmetries, including the proposed generalization of Bondi-Metzner-Sachs generators. Furthermore, the paper establishes a correspondence between the superalgebra's charges and the AdS/CFT side's supertranslation symmetry and its associated central extension, also linking them to the scalar field's monodromy and charge flux.

In a kidney transplant scenario involving living donors and multiple recipients,
we model the decision-making process using a Markov Decision Process that takes
into account various incompatibility factors as states. This model enables the
evaluation of a successful transplant match and helps identify the optimal policy
outcomes. Our research demonstrates the impact of different modeling approaches
on the resulting policy, showing that incorporating incompatibility as a state
variable significantly influences the cost of excluding certain donors.

This research explores the connection between Hidden Markov Models and Long Short-Term Memory Models, focusing on how their hidden state structures differ. While not all HSMMs can be represented as LSTMs, we identify specific conditions under which this is possible, and demonstrate that on-line linearly constrained HSMMs have LSTM equivalents.
We investigate the compactness and membership in Schatten classes of composition operators between weighted Bergman spaces by applying this analysis.

This paper explores the effectiveness of compressed neural networks for text classification by examining the impact of reduced parameter count on model performance across multiple text datasets. We assess the performance of different compressed models, including those with a limited number of filters, a compressed channel structure, and sparse models, and find that a specific model with sparse channels achieves a notable balance between compression and accuracy in each of our evaluations.

In the 2021 Snowmass town meeting, a working group on computational tools and software emphasized the growing importance of software development in high-energy physics research, with a pressing need for novel approaches to leveraging computational expertise and fostering collaboration among researchers to better analyze data and streamline experimental processes. Building on this foundation, we introduce the concept of a software engineer as a vital member of the HEP research community, with a unique set of challenges and opportunities that warrant further exploration. We identify key factors that can facilitate the widespread adoption of this role and propose specific initiatives to be explored further by the community.

This article expands our understanding of Howe curves, defining a new category
of curves, generalized Howe curves, whose polynomial functions create
decomposable Richelot isogenies. We develop a systematic approach to
construct these curves and demonstrate how each pair of decomposed curves
shares a common isomorphism, resulting in distinct field extensions. Furthermore,
we establish the complex multiplication of these generalized curves.

A recent discovery of a large group of 19 newly identified magnetic hot subdwarfs through high-resolution spectropolarimetric analysis has provided fresh insights into these enigmatic stars. The research revealed low levels of surface iron abundance in these magnetic stars, contradicting existing theoretical models that had previously predicted significantly higher abundance levels. This deviation raises intriguing questions about the underlying magnetic mechanism and the evolutionary processes that shape these stars. The research also identified a distinct subset of 13 stars that exhibit particularly strong magnetic fields and unusual chemical compositions, warranting further investigation into their characteristics. The full dataset of 19 stars is available electronically, allowing for a more comprehensive examination of these fascinating celestial objects.

We establish error approximations for the low-rank approximation of a matrix using principles from invariant matrix theory, which can be applied to all symmetric gauge spaces without requiring specific matrix structure. This framework also allows us to extend low-rank approximation to tensor objects, specifically by approximating tensor ranks, which is achieved through an examination of the minimal rank of tensor products. Notably, our findings on low-rank tensor approximation align with the framework developed by Chenu et al. in an earlier work.
