Extractive question-answering systems can be improved by pre-training on various languages, but a more effective method is training models with large volumes of data from specific languages, such as Romanian. By leveraging an open-source framework, OpenQuadruplet, we fine-tune RoBERTa for Romanian EQA and incorporate an active learning framework to increase the available data without needing a massive amount of human-annotated examples. By utilizing this pipeline, we successfully create a highly accurate Romanian EQA system, achieving 82.3% F1 score. The system is now integrated into the Rumex platform, which provides a comprehensive tool for analyzing and summarizing political texts. The framework is adaptable to any language, making it a valuable resource for developing question-answering models.

The distribution of baryons not accounted for in the Cosmic Web's matter power spectrum has long been a mystery. We've found a direct link between baryon dark matter clustering and the distribution of baryons not seen in the SIMBA galaxy formation model. Our analysis of these missing baryons shows they follow the same clustering pattern as dark matter but avoid areas occupied by galaxies and hot gas. A comparison with the distribution of galaxies reveals the baryon mode is more sensitive to environment than the galaxy mode. We also discovered that the distribution of baryons not seen is highly non-linear and influenced by feedback, suggesting it could be the cause of some observed features. Our results imply that the distribution of missing baryons could be the underlying reason for some of the small-scale issues with the matter power spectrum in the SIMBA model.

We've developed an algorithm to approximate the treewidth of a given graph, taking around O(2^0.28k + k) moves as part of the branching process, with move complexity also bounded by a multiple of O((2^0.28k + k) \log n) and a polynomial number of operations, where k is the treewidth and n is the graph size. This surpasses the previous time complexity of the Geelen et al. algorithm, which was O(2^{\log 2 + \log k) + k).

The rate at which stars are consumed by Tidal Disruption Events greatly surpasses the rate at which those stars are destroyed through supernovae. Observations of supernovae in galaxies that have recently ceased star formation reveal a significant imbalance between the number of supernovae observed and the number predicted based on the TDE rate. This discrepancy suggests that most supernovae observed are not occurring within recent star-forming periods, but rather in earlier, more prolonged periods. This hypothesis is supported by the findings of a study on supernovae in galaxies that have recently ceased star formation, which indicate that 60-90% of these supernovae are occurring in epochs that are at least 10-30 million years in the past. This has significant implications for the study of supernovae, as it means they are providing insights into a period of star-formation that is at least three times farther back than the time of their most recent burst.

In 5G New Radio systems, dynamic resource allocation within a cell is a pressing challenge due to the growing number of access users and their fluctuating data demands. This study presents a novel approach to resource allocation, applying deep reinforcement learning to an actor-critic style scheduling system. This method optimizes resource allocation based on network conditions and cell requirements, allowing it to dynamically adjust to changing scenarios without requiring explicit programming. Experimental results based on extensive network trials demonstrate that learning-based scheduling methods surpass traditional approaches in achieving efficient resource distribution. Notably, our approach enhances average user throughput by 17.4% and 12.9% over baseline methods, with no compromise on 5G quality of service requirements.

In recent years, significant advancements in quality estimation have been made, with a notable shift from sentence-level to word-level approaches. This transition has led to a proposal for a new challenge that contrasts quality estimation models as either being used at the sentence or word level. This distinction seems to define two different purposes of quality estimation - one as a tool for quality assessment and the other as a training aid. This paper argues that these two purposes are not mutually exclusive and can be incorporated into a single quality estimation model. To test this hypothesis, we propose a dual-task quality estimation model that simultaneously performs two tasks: evaluating quality at the sentence level and training models with word-level quality labels. We demonstrate that a quality estimation model can handle multiple tasks and provide labels to support both purposes, with the outcome of a study that compared our proposed model to a single-task model, which showed improved results in word-level quality estimation.

A novel Kerr-de Sitter black hole solution has been discovered through a practical application of the Klein-Gordon equation in the presence of a nonlinear source, where its asymptotic behavior is analytically expressed as a series of new hypergeometric functions. The study then examines the dynamics of photon geodesics around the new black hole and finds that its shadow has distinct characteristics, such as a shadow radius, position angle, and area, which are all dependent on the new non-trivial parameter of its asymptotic series, demonstrating significant differences from the original Kerr-de Sitter black hole solution.

Numerous studies have shown that a particular dynamic formulation of relativistic hydrodynamics is prone to inaccuracies and issues of numerical instability. In an effort to address this, a novel flux-conservative relativistic hydrodynamics formulation is introduced and its effectiveness is explored. Building upon first-order upwind methods, this flux-conservative formulation is shown to be an extension of existing relativistic hydrodynamics models, incorporating a dynamic flow direction and ensuring that physical entropy levels are preserved. Numerical simulations conducted for a variety of challenging scenarios, including relativistic shock waves and ultra-relativistic jets, reveal significant improvements in accuracy and stability compared to traditional methods.

The $D_{sJ}$ states, which consist of four distinct states, were previously discovered through the $D^+ K^0_{\rm S}$ decay process.  A recent analysis of $D^+ K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ decays of the $D_{sJ}(2860)$ and $D_{sJ}(2860)^*$ states by the BESIII detector revealed the presence of several $D_{sJ}$ states, which include the previously unobserved $D^*_{s2}(2573)$ state.  The results of this research are presented in the form of a Riemann sum, which shows that the $D^*_{s2}(2573)$ state can be identified as a $D^*_{s2}(2573)$ and that the previously identified $D^*_{s1}(2860)$ and $D^0_{s1}(2860)$ states can be seen as two possible solutions for this state, which are $D^*_{s1}(2860)$ and $D^0_{s1}(2860)$.  The results of this research are consistent with the results of previous studies, including the results of the LHCb collaboration.

We propose a new method for calculating the fractal dimensions of functions defined on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket, with specific focus on polynomial and analytic functions. This approach enables the estimation of certain key topological and algebraic parameters of these functions, leveraging a combination of spectral theory, the Frobenius-Perron operator, and a dimension reduction technique. To illustrate its effectiveness, we apply our method to the Haar polynomial and analyze functions constructed from rational expressions, ultimately obtaining consistent results for the fractal dimension.

The ability to create and understand questions is crucial for effective communication and is a vital component of natural language processing. Currently, available large language models are limited in their capacity to generate questions based on visual information alone, resulting in output that is often irrelevant or incoherent. In order to address this issue, our research investigates the potential benefits of providing direction to question generation models when they operate in a visual domain. We introduce a novel, multi-step approach that combines visual information with a large language model, starting with the use of an unsupervised method to extract meaningful information from the image and then leveraging a large language model to create visually-based questions. By testing our approach, called Image Guided Question Generation, we found that it significantly enhances the quality of the generated questions from both human assessments and automatic metrics, resulting in more coherent, relevant, and meaningful questions.

The dark matter halo's density profile is a crucial aspect of the universe's structure and its constituent's behavior. The core's size in isolated dwarf galaxies is a key indicator of the substructure of these dark matter halos. The core's size in these systems is primarily determined by the properties of their dwarf galaxies. The study of dwarf galaxies' internal structure has led to a finding that their dark matter density profile is dependent on their stellar mass. The analysis of 18 isolated dwarf galaxies from the IllustrisTNG simulations shows that their dark matter density profile is a function of their stellar mass. The core's size in these systems follows a power-law relationship with the stellar mass. The study suggests that the dark matter halo's properties are influenced by the presence of baryons in these systems, particularly in low-mass halos. The study's findings have significant implications for the characterization of dwarf galaxies in real-world observations.

The quasipure literal elimination procedure is a method for simplifying Boolean formulas by removing variables from clauses in sequence until a stable solution is reached, preserving the input formula's meaning. In contrast to the pure literal elimination method, this procedure considers clauses as part of the input, rather than isolating individual variables. We investigate the relationship between these two methods, focusing on how their output formulas differ and whether these differences can be mitigated within the quasipure procedure.

This research paper introduces a novel theorem of evolutionary game theory, extending the traditional Folk Theorem to encompass a broader range of games. Building upon the concept of backward induction, the theorem reveals that nearly all outcomes in rational evolutionary games are attainable pure Nash equilibria, including scenarios where all parties do not necessarily lose. The proposed theorem is substantiated through two computational methods: a direct algorithm and an alternative proof leveraging the properties of rational evolutionary games.

This study introduces a multivariate regression tree algorithm that generates estimates for multiple variables by splitting data across all target attributes. It demonstrates how these estimates can be viewed as a weighted average of target-specific split values, showing that distinct splits across different variables are statistically independent. Additionally, it derives a multivariate analogue of the univariate simple regression equation and identifies key constraints necessary for the development of regression trees based on absolute mean squared error. Furthermore, it proposes two approaches for constructing regression trees: a basic method and a more complex recursive partitioning method.

This study presents a communication-efficient electric vehicle charging algorithm, referred to as ComCerts, for enhanced efficiency in vehicle-to-grid charging. The algorithm's communication management strategy allows the charging server to decide whether to request power from EVs, with the goal of optimizing overall energy efficiency. The ComCerts algorithm has been experimentally verified to achieve identical charging results to a previous, communication-intensive approach while utilizing up to 90% less communication.

Accurate comparison of materials' properties relies on reliable and reproducible results, a requirement that is often compromised by discrepancies arising from the use of varying density functionals in simulations. This work highlights the significance of minimizing numerical errors to ensure consistency in results, particularly when different density functionals are employed. A test case of silicon nanotubes is used to demonstrate how the choice of density functional affects the calculation of electronic properties. Furthermore, this work introduces the concept of "functional independence" and proposes methods for improving reproducibility, including the utilization of multiple density functionals to gauge the stability of results and the application of a correction term to reduce numerical errors.

Bacteria and other microbes have a metabolic function that defines the resources they need and produce, which we call the metabolic niche space. This metabolic space is determined by the bacteria's ability to use and produce resources, which can be influenced by the environment, host, and social interactions. To investigate the expansion of the metabolic niche space, we analyzed data from the Human Microbiome Project over a two-year period, which showed that the metabolic space is larger in children than in adults, especially in individuals with a healthier microbiome. This increase in metabolic diversity was linked to the bacteria's ability to adapt and respond to environmental changes, which could provide new insights for developing targeted therapies to modify the metabolic activity of specific microbe groups and improve human health.

The growing reliance on energy has led to increased focus on monitoring building systems to optimize energy consumption. This study presents an innovative model-based approach that enhances monitoring efficiency through the application of the Symbolic Aggregate Approximation method. Using the Alpha model, the proposed algorithm transforms high-dimensional sensor data into lower-dimensional, non-linear state space representations. This enables the estimation of unknown system parameters, facilitating the detection of anomalies without requiring access to system equations. The approach was validated using data collected from a real-world university campus with multiple buildings.

A small number of SLSNe have hydrogen-poor spectra, but their exact origins are unclear. Research suggests these SLSNe may stem from stripped envelope hydrogen stars that evolve into hydrogen-poor progenitors. In this study, we utilize binary star population synthesis models to investigate the connection between these SLSNe and pre-SN binary systems. We discovered that a significant portion of SLSNe with hydrogen-poor spectra can be explained by pre-SN binary systems. We also found that a pre-SN mass of approximately 55 M solar masses is crucial for accurately predicting the observed SLSN diversity. Furthermore, our results indicate that a pre-SN binary system's envelope mass is directly linked to the observed SLSN properties, providing a potential explanation for the diversity of hydrogen-poor SLSNe.

In modern times, the demand for smaller, highly sensitive magnetic storage devices is increasing, it's essential to explore the fundamental properties of modern magnetic materials. This study focuses on the magnetic properties of a specific type of two-dimensional magnet made of a material that exhibits strong interactions between magnetic atoms. Utilizing a quantum master equation approach, we developed a detailed theoretical framework to analyze the complex behavior of these magnets in both classical and quantum systems. We investigated how temperature affects the magnetic hysteresis in a classical model, revealing a transition from irregular to smooth curves as temperature increases. We also studied the root cause of the magnetic switching time in both classical and quantum systems, discovering that increasing temperature causes a shift in the switching dynamics. Furthermore, we discovered that in a certain range of temperatures, the magnetic switching time becomes more consistent. We also analyzed the effect of temperature on the energy barrier that hinders magnetic switching in both classical and quantum systems.

Syntactic analysis, a core challenge in natural language processing, necessitates a deep understanding of constituent hierarchies.  Despite significant breakthroughs in neural networks, determining constituent boundaries and their respective structures remains a difficult problem.  Conventional approaches rely on hand-engineered distance-based algorithms, which are susceptible to errors.  In this study, a novel syntax model called VGSyn is introduced, leveraging visually grounded neural networks to induce constituency grammar directly from images.  VGSyn employs a unique, contrastive training framework that leverages the contrast between processed words to identify word-level hierarchies.  Through its contrastive objective, VGSyn identifies and categorizes both content words and prepositions into separate branches.  As a result, VGSyn outperforms traditional methods in parsing accuracy, particularly when content words and prepositions are in separate branches, and significantly reduces the risk of inductive bias errors.  Furthermore, VGSyn demonstrates a significant advantage over previous syntax models in parsing novel, unseen sentences.

A widespread issue exists among attribution methods, which fail to perform well when applied to different datasets than they were trained on, leading to inconsistent results across different datasets used in the literature.  To investigate this, a study was conducted to see how well established attribution methods perform on a range of datasets including CIFAR-10, MNIST, and ImageNet, with the results showing that these methods are highly dataset-dependent and can't effectively be transferred.  In an attempt to address this limitation, a method was developed that allows the learning of dataset-specific properties by neural networks, enabling them to effectively operate across different datasets, with the results demonstrating that when these networks were used, a range of attribution methods performed better on these diverse datasets, with the results showing significant improvements on ImageNet using traditional methods.

In models of wormholes that have a symmetry of rotational symmetry, the appearance of a secondary shadow in an observer's view is investigated. An in-depth examination is conducted to see if the observed image of a source has distinct features, such as double shadows, double photon spheres, and enhanced images. It is found that the observed shadow in a distant location is larger and more dim than the original shadow, with the former being wider than the latter but less intense. Moreover, the observed shadow in a distant location can act as a secondary photon sphere that occurs outside the primary shadow. An illustration is given using static models of wormholes that have a connection to general relativity, specifically the Schwarzschild black hole and the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole.

We introduce an innovative subadditive estimate for permutations and apply it to various forms of the permanent $\mathrm{per}$, ultimately yielding new estimates for the permanent in several instances. Specifically, this approach allows us to extend the domain of application for the Holder inequality for the permanent in two key ways: it accommodates non-negative matrix entries and non-integer p values. Moreover, this estimate provides a simplified proof for the weighted version of the Holder inequality for the permanent, which was previously established by Harcholacis and Seeger. Our results also enable us to establish a submultiplicative bias for permutations and develop a novel spectral analysis of the permanent in the context of non-negative matrices. Furthermore, this approach leads to new bounds for the Ryser conjecture and the permanent in matrices with low rank and non-negative entries.

We explore a class of trimmer models on a triangular lattice, drawing inspiration from Z-invariant dimer and chessboard models. By introducing edge weights that alternate, these trimmer models can be viewed as a combination of Z or chessboard models. We derive the partition functions and free energies of these models, converting them back to the original parametrization to obtain solutions in terms of modular functions. Notably, the resulting models exhibit non-chiral properties and belong to the same family as the well-known planar dilute Ising model.

This paper addresses the issue of target-free detection by a supporting agent, which requires identifying unknown target samples and distinguishing them from known ones. The proposed method centers on learning a distinctive feature for the unknown target through collaborative interaction with other known targets. By analyzing the interaction data with k targets, the agent calculates and compares the differences between the known and unknown targets in a shared feature space. As a result, the agent can effectively distinguish between known and unknown targets without requiring prior target knowledge, as long as there is sufficient interaction data with known targets. The proposed method's effectiveness is confirmed through numerical simulations using various interaction environments and target types.

This paper introduces a novel neural network approach for 3D reconstruction of vehicles from a single monocular camera image. The method addresses challenges associated with limited field of view and occlusions by utilizing a multi-branch convolutional neural network to normalize and regularize vehicle shapes. The regularized shapes are then combined with monocular depth estimates to produce a complete 3D model. The method also incorporates occlusion-aware vehicle shape prediction using a conditional generative adversarial network and optimizes depth and shape regularization using a multi-task loss function. Comprehensive experiments on both real and synthetic vehicle datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms previous methods.

This research introduces an innovative method for automatically designing query graph structures from natural language inputs for query-based tasks such as question answering. Our proposed approach is the first to integrate a discrete variational autoencoder trained at a graph level with a differentiable discrete mapping approach for generating graph tokens. By utilizing this variational autoencoder, we can represent a query as a query graph, where the token alignment is recognized through the generated nodes and edges. Our experimental outcomes on Complex Question Answering indicate that our method significantly outperforms the existing token-level query-to-graph embedding approaches.

This paper revisits the core issue of developing a suitable generalization of the Cauchy-Reimer model, a simple symmetric substitution cryptosystem where all symbols are affected with equal likelihood. A generalization to infinite alphabets, denoted $\mathbb{X}_{\infty}$, is proposed where each symbol $X_i$ in the original alphabet is replaced by an infinite set of distinct symbols $X_i = \{X_{i_1}, X_{i_2}, \ldots\}$, effectively treating these as separate elements. This new framework is used to generalize the Cauchy-Reimer model, leading to the development of a new substitution cryptosystem, referred to as CRCR$_{\infty}$, on infinite alphabets. A key aspect of CRCR$_{\infty}$ is that it can be represented as a weighted transformation on infinite symbolic spaces, with the weights being real numbers ranging from 0 to 1. A necessary and sufficient condition is established to ensure the ergodicity of these weighted dynamical systems.

This study investigates two strategies for identifying specific meanings for ambiguous named entities within Wikipedia's knowledge graph. One strategy leverages user link annotations on Wikipedia pages, whereas the other employs supplementary data derived from external knowledge graphs. We demonstrate that a unified framework, combining both approaches and employing random walk-based aggregation, yields superior results according to recall and mean reciprocal rank metrics.

We have calculated the one-loop contribution to the photonic part of the $S$, $T$, and $U$ oblique parameters arising from the electroweak self-energies of the gauge bosons, considering the full set of one-loop diagrams. This calculation is performed without imposing the condition of flavor universality on the fermionic electroweak couplings. In the context of a general model, we have derived the expressions for $S$, $T$, and $U$ in terms of specific loop integrals, and then approximated them in the framework of a four-structure-point model. Our findings are presented in a simplified, flavor-universal scenario, and we also provide a direct comparison with the results obtained from the standard model formulae, derived via on-shell renormalization, in addition to the results from the $\bar{\rm MS}$ subtraction scheme.

Dynamic view generation, which involves creating novel views from a set of input images, is a complex problem that necessitates the use of additional data for training. However, we've discovered that incorporating auxiliary losses rooted in spatial and temporal regularization techniques significantly improves the learning process when working with a single video source. By implementing these constraints, we're able to develop highly coherent, smooth, and realistic animations that can be manipulated interactively, all without requiring a vast dataset. Instead, we've developed a framework for training neural dynamic models using a single video, which enables the extension of learned representations through data augmentation and efficient rendering of novel animations. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate our approach's effectiveness and we provide a detailed analysis of its components and applications. Furthermore, we've developed an interactive demonstrative application that can be freely explored online at https://www.computingroutines.com/animdiff/.

This study examines the differential equation $dy = \sum_{n \geq 1} g_n(t, y) \, dt + \sum_{n \geq 1} f_n(y) \, dz^{n}$, 
where the right-hand side is defined in terms of a branched rough path $z$ and its values at specific points. We investigate the impact of the path's regularity on the solution's behavior and derive a criterion for its continuity based on the given functions' properties. This criterion holds under both the framework of Mabuchi-Bauer-Martinez-Ruth, and the framework of Allamore, Clerc, and Cooper. We also demonstrate that a solution exists and is unique within the space of paths with a specific regularity, provided that the functions satisfy certain conditions of boundedness and subexponentiation.

This research paper outlines a method for creating Hermite and Laguerre-type probability distributions that result from applying a non-linear transformation to an existing random model derived from grain data. This approach leverages the combinatorial properties of combinatorial random models to provide novel representations of orthogonal polynomials, such as Charlier and Meixner polynomials, through the use of generating functions like Mehler's formula. Additionally, it offers a novel method for obtaining Hermite and Laguerre-type special functions like the Laplace transform, utilizing the theory of discrete random models to derive novel representations. The paper includes explicit examples of such probability distributions for specific models, illustrating their practical applications in various probabilistic models.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces-assisted networks hold great potential for substantial enhancements in wireless network efficiency. Real-world deployment of these networks requires an in-depth understanding of the challenges associated with the practical implementation of RIS-assisted systems. This study delves into the fundamental issues hindering the effective deployment of RIS-assisted networks. Initially, we examine the requirements for seamless network operation and identify the difficulties in achieving these goals. Next, we address the complexities in designing and simulating RIS-assisted networks. Furthermore, we discuss the intricacies of modeling and analyzing RIS-assisted systems. Ultimately, we discuss the complexities in implementing and evaluating RIS-assisted networks.

We introduce a novel approach to simplify complex stochastic systems, converting them into simplified Markov chain models with significantly reduced computational costs. These simplified models maintain key characteristics, such as mean and variance, while incorporating a simplified reaction rate formalism that preserves its original dynamics with high accuracy. We validate our approach by first applying it to a basic mass-action system, achieving results consistent with theoretical expectations. We then apply it to a more challenging HIV infection model, where our simplified model accurately replicates the effects of antiretroviral therapy compared to a detailed simulation.

Most current studies on quantizing neural networks are based on a single approach that either uses fixed weights or adjusts weights within predetermined ranges. However, this approach often fails to accurately identify the optimal weight ranges during the training process. Our research introduces a novel method called cyclic training, which involves repeatedly training low-bit quantized models and then converting them back to full-precision models. This process allows us to assess the performance of low-bit models and identify optimal weight rounding parameters. Our method is an automated approach that does not require manual intervention. Our experiments on image classification tasks showed that using this method can consistently achieve high accuracy with extremely low-bit weights.

The majority of Type Ia supernovae are thought to originate from the merger of two white dwarfs. The mass of the more massive white dwarf and the characteristics of the orbit of the binary system can be determined through the explosion's kinetic energy. The mass of the less massive white dwarf, the mass of the companion star, and the resulting supernova kinetic energy are all interrelated. These parameters are influenced by the properties of the white dwarfs' progenitors, the characteristics of the companion stars, and the resulting supernova kinetic energy. Our study investigates the conditions under which these white dwarf mergers occur, focusing on the single mass ratio scenario. We find that the conditions under which these mergers occur differ significantly from those of the single degenerate type Ia supernova channel. Specifically, the mass of the less massive white dwarf must be below a certain threshold, the mass of the companion star is restricted to avoid excessive mass loss, and the resulting supernova kinetic energy is highly dependent on the mass of the less massive white dwarf. Our results also indicate that the single mass ratio scenario cannot explain the entire population of Type Ia supernovae, as it fails to account for the observed range of kinetic energies.

In real-world machine learning applications, data often arrives in non-uniform chunks, and our training strategies need to adapt accordingly. This adaptability is essential for online learning, but research has yet to fully explore how the distribution of chunk sizes impacts model training. This work delves into the relationship between learning rates and data distributions, offering a theoretical and empirical analysis of the effects of different data distributions on training resilience and performance. Our experiments reveal that the size of data chunks significantly influences learning rate scheduling, and our proposed schedule-free training method, LRE, demonstrates superior results in both uniform and non-uniform data settings. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis reveals that the optimal learning rate schedule is highly dependent on the distribution of data chunks.

A global vaccine effort is underway, having vaccinated over three-quarters of the population in countries like the United States, China, and India, albeit with significant progress disparities.  A novel approach is presented in this study to streamline and make vaccination records transparent in settings with limited resources.  Digital Vaccine Passports, also known as COVID-19 vaccination certificates, have been introduced in several countries, including the US, UK, and India, despite facing controversy over their legitimacy.  A new framework is proposed to make vaccination verifiable, secure, blockchain-based, and accessible to the broader public, thus enabling individuals to securely manage their vaccination records.  Moreover, the framework is designed to facilitate interoperability across countries, making it easier to demonstrate vaccination status to countries requiring it for travel and allowing for easy data sharing and retrieval.  A novel blockchain-based system is proposed to demonstrate the feasibility of this framework, providing an auditable record of vaccinations, secure storage, and transparent data.

This study's primary goal is to gain insight into text datasets' intrinsic structure. To achieve this, we utilize sentence embeddings and identify clusters in the resulting space to determine topic classifications. We develop an unsupervised method to determine if a set of sentences belongs to a topic class, by determining the probability that a specific cluster will produce a topic classification. This approach is based on a previously established model for identifying topic distributions in sentences. Our evaluation involves multiple datasets and a comparison with supervised topic modeling techniques. The results show that the proposed method can effectively determine topic classifications with good accuracy, even without supervision.

We investigate the diffusion of identical particles within a randomly structured environment.  Utilizing the Wigner function, an analytical solution to the Schrödinger equation for a system of independent particles is derived.  By analyzing the phase space distribution function, the diffusion dynamics of the particles are characterized in terms of their mean displacement, movement, and confinement.  Through this analysis, the diffusion coefficient is expressed as a function of the confinement scale and the energy of the particles, indicating that diffusion is effectively localized when the confinement scale is on the order of or smaller than the thermal de Broglie wavelength.  Furthermore, the effects of anti-symmetrizing the wave function on the dynamics of the particles are examined.

Our research focuses on how the spin evolves over time in a system where spin is connected to nuclear spin through a long-range magnetic field. The spin system consists of transverse components, and we explore how the spin evolves differently based on its orientation. The spin evolution has two different behaviors in the long-term and short-term cases. The spin evolution with the same orientation tends to relax more quickly and uniformly over time in the long-term case, but this relaxation effect is influenced by the spin's dynamic movement. However, this relaxation effect is influenced by the spin's dynamic movement in a way that is dependent on its orientation. The spin evolution with opposing orientations tends to relax more slowly and unevenly over time in the short-term case, but this relaxation effect is influenced by the spin's counter-movement. However, this opposing movement affects the spin evolution with opposing orientations. Our investigation focuses on the return probability and energy dynamics within a periodically driven conformal field theory (CDT). Following an initial period where the return probability exhibits a characteristic power-law increase with linearly decreasing energy, a more complex regime is observed above a specific crossover point where the return probability grows exponentially with time and is accompanied by an unbounded growth in energy levels. Interestingly, below this point, the return probability and energy follow distinct time-dependent power-law patterns, with return probability growing faster and energy levels increasing more slowly. Additionally, we identify a scaling behavior in the return probability and energy, along with a specific time-dependent correlation function, which exhibits a characteristic oscillatory pattern. Our findings also imply the presence of an underlying time-invariant structure within this periodically driven CDT.

This research investigates the potential of the compressed sensing concept to enhance the effectiveness of a fusion algorithm in a multi-sensor setup. The proposed fusion strategy employs a single measurement from each sensor, passing them through distinct calibration and pre-processing stages. A decoder then combines these pre-processed measurements to produce a complete representation of the state. The preprocessed sensor data is then fed into a Kalman filter for state estimation. Simulation results on a nonlinear benchmark problem demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves comparable performance to a standard fusion algorithm that utilizes full measurements, while reducing communication costs by half.

The Standard Model's precise prediction of the $CPT$ phase is a crucial test for beyond-SM physics and can be enhanced in specific cases by combining inputs from various $CPT$ measurements. A notable example is the $CPT$ phase derived from combining measurements of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, the NA8/$K^0_K^0$ decay, and the $K^0_{S,D}$ decay, which has been experimentally verified to be consistent. We report a high-precision $CPT$ phase prediction of $346.046(28)$ meV from a unitary triangle analysis, which significantly surpasses the previous measurement of the $K^0_{S,D}$ phase. This improvement is achieved through the application of new renormalization group running to $CPT$-odd matrix elements. Furthermore, we have investigated the unitary triangle in the $\Delta I=1/2$ rule context, which has potential applications in beyond-SM physics studies and can be complemented by our new $CPT$ phase prediction.

This research investigates the design of distributed control systems comprising sensors, a controller, and actuators, with the goal of optimizing performance despite limited communication resources. We focus on a broad class of nonlinear systems and identify the most effective strategies for sensing, communication, and control to strike a balance between performance and reduced data exchange. The investigation reveals the trade-offs between communication costs and overall system performance, as well as the optimal distribution of sensing and control responsibilities within multilevel hierarchical systems.

A novel, efficient method is introduced for the Gibbs sampler to produce a multi-Bernoulli birth distribution that can be shared across multiple sensors in a multi-sensor system, significantly improving upon the standard birth process. The proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in computational complexity, typically by a factor of the number of sensors involved. A mathematical analysis is conducted to confirm the method's accuracy, reliability, and improved efficiency, with numerical simulations demonstrating the practical benefits of this advancement in sensor management strategies.

In this study, we investigate the feature correlations present in YCOG, a vast typological knowledge base containing data from approximately 550 languages. YCOG's structured nature and diverse data create an ideal environment to explore the complex interactions between linguistic characteristics, which can be difficult to dissect individually. By utilizing this dataset, we aim to demonstrate how the connections between features can be leveraged to address key challenges in typological data sets, encompassing issues like data quality, annotation consistency, and the challenges posed by languages with limited resources.

We examine the theoretical foundations of advanced off-policy evaluation techniques and investigate the statistical significance of various hyper-parameters and design factors influencing the performance of the propensity score class. Our analysis encompasses key statistical attributes such as the bias, mean square error, and optimal sample size in both fixed design and random design settings. We also compare and contrast our findings with the existing empirical literature on non-parametric regression, highlighting the need for a balanced approach to bias and variance. Moreover, our study yields design guidelines for optimal sample size, leading to the development of a new tool, MSVR, which enhances design selection for various off-policy evaluation techniques.

The main objective of this research is to develop a Bayesian framework to model the variability in fermentation outputs resulting from known active agents. By incorporating fermentation data from multiple trials with varying agent doses, the proposed approach aims to quantify the uncertainty associated with the variability. This method can be applied to evaluate the relative potency of agents across different fermentation batches. Additionally, the model enables the prediction of the distribution of outputs for new experiments, provided the doses and number of experiments for the new trial are known. Furthermore, the approach allows for the estimation of the 95th percentile of the distribution, which is analogous to determining the ED50, but for the variability rather than the overall output. The proposed method is demonstrated through a case study using actual data from a clinical trial conducted by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

The polaron problem is re-examined using a specific approach that involves
analytic continuation of Feynman graphs, with a particular focus on the
relationship between momentum and the square of the electron's mass. This
approach allows the effective mass of the electron to be treated as variable
and dependent on its momentum, with a term of the form (p/m)^2 added to the
mass, where p represents the electron's momentum. This modification is found
to be proportional to the real part of the self-energy, with a specific limit
that corresponds to the well-known polaron effective mass. The resulting
mass term is then compared to the widely used Fröhlich self-energy approach
and the concept of "quasiparticles" with a variable effective mass.

The decay of electric flux in a force-free electrodynamics context is examined under conditions of constant magnetic field strength. It is discovered that the flux decays at a rate proportional to $t^{-1/3}$ for a magnetic field that remains constant in time, and $t^{-1/2}$ for a magnetically accelerating grid when $B \sim t^{\sigma}$ with $-1/2<\sigma<1/2$. A theory for flux decay is formulated and its range of applicability determined.

A well-known thought experiment involving Schr\"{o}dinger's cat illustrates the concept that a quantum system can still be in a superposition even when it interacts with the macroscopic environment. This idea challenges the notion that the interaction with the environment turns a cat into alive from a "dead" state. To clarify the application of quantum superposition to large-scale systems, we'll use the example of a cat being poisoned and sealed in a box.

We investigate the minimal periodic patterns that combine to form a given pattern $P$, focusing on periodicity constraints and the shortest possible decomposition lengths. This investigation leads to several general conjectures and the derivation of complexity formulas for specific $P$ patterns. Notably, a conjecture by Szabados leads to a complexity formula for square patterns with a 2x2 structure, and our findings suggest that the validity of this conjecture depends on the variety of patterns considered. Additionally, a minimum of three different decomposition types is shown to be possible for certain 3x3 patterns. To further analyze these decompositions, a systematic approach is developed to generate all periodic patterns of a given size. This method is demonstrated using a 5x5 pattern, resulting in the recovery of known minimal decompositions and the discovery of 11 new ones. An example of a 5x5 pattern with a minimum decomposition of 9 elements is provided.

The Gromov-Hausdorff distance serves as a natural method to gauge the similarity of two bounded metric spaces, with its introduction by Gromov demonstrating its ability to capture key characteristics of bounded metric spaces. Building on this concept, I will extend the Gromov-Hausdorff distance to generalized bimetric spaces, defined as metric spaces incorporating additional pseudometrics, and will generalize the definition of geodesic between subsets of such spaces as the intersection of their respective pseudometrics. Key findings include the proof that the proposed distance aligns with the Hamming distance in graph contexts, and that it corresponds with the original Gromov-Hausdorff distance in specific scenarios, like when non-Archimedean pseudometrics are absent. Additionally, I will investigate the impact of varying the space's geometry on the resulting distance.

For the resolgent of a first order elliptic operator with divergence form, 
considering a parameter-dependent self-adjoint matrix within the underlying 
function space, our study demonstrates that an optimal approximation of the 
resolvent holds when the remainder term is inversely proportional to the 
square of this parameter when the matrix is sufficiently close to being positive 
definite, and this remainder term is of order one with respect to the parameter.

In recent years, the use of dialogue systems has grown significantly, and as a result, the need for benchmarking and evaluating these systems has become more critical. This paper presents a new framework for assessing dialogue systems through the creation of a formal dialogue states database. This database enables the use of automated testing methods to evaluate dialogue systems in a more objective and efficient manner. To facilitate the use of the database, we also release a set of benchmark scripts.

A novel runtime technique for applications that use SMT solving in their analysis has been developed. It can improve performance by reducing the number of solvers needed, by initially eliminating unsolvable instances, thereby preventing the stack from overflowing or consuming excessive resources. Additionally, the technique provides a memory-safe operation for large datasets that generate an immense number of instances. The technique, known as Smt-Switch, dynamically switches between two SMT solvers based on the type of analysis required. It achieves a better balance between the two solvers by dynamically switching between them based on the number of instances generated by each, there by improving the performance of the solver. Experimental evaluations on a variety of benchmarks have shown a significant speedup of the technique, with a maximum speedup of 7.4x over traditional SMT-based analysis.

The OPPQ method, which uses orthogonal polynomials to quantize wavefunctions, has been applied in various cases including exact and approximate solutions. In this work, the quantization is extended to all eigenstates in one-dimensional time-dependent Schrodinger equations with any regular potential using an adaptive quadrature method. By comparing the results with other popular methods, OPPQ was found to provide a good approximation of time-dependent wavefunctions with high precision. Moreover, OPPQ outperformed other methods in its stability and convergence for states with exact quantum numbers, while only showing moderate convergence for non-quantum number states.

Deep neural networks have been found to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, which pose a significant challenge to deploying models in safety-critical applications.  Recent research has focused on using adversarial examples to train robust models, which however often require substantial amounts of labeled data and large budgets for training.  A novel approach to address this limitation involves adapting a model's input resolution, which allows it to process lower-resolution versions of inputs while still achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with lower training budgets. This flexibility enables the use of these models in low-resource settings, which can then be further fortified by adversarial training. Our experiments demonstrate that such an approach improves robustness in models adapted for low-power hardware implementations.

The surface of a star in a close binary system can exhibit unique patterns due to its rotation and interaction with its companion. Using high-resolution images from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, we analyzed the chromospheric activity of a rapidly rotating M-dwarf binary system, with a focus on a secondary star influenced by its primary's gravitational pull. Our observations show that the secondary star's rotation is synchronized with its orbital motion, and we detected varying levels of chromospheric activity across our two observation periods. We have analyzed the existence and stability of charged scalar clouds perched at the event horizon of a spherically symmetric black hole, with a specific type of self-interacting potential at the heart of the model. Our study reveals that its unique properties enable the formation of distinct scalar clouds that aren't possible to achieve with other types of potentials, including static, time-independent configurations. Furthermore, our research explores their stability, with key numerical values obtained through computational analysis.

We examine how the phases that violate CP symmetry in neutrino mixing between active and sterile species influence neutrino properties and their presence within first-generation degenerate Majoron bosons.  By considering the lightest Majoron boson as the dark matter particle, we investigate the constraints on the model's parameters that can be placed by current and future observations.  Both wave-like and scalar-like scenarios are studied, with the results indicating that the phases and sterile neutrino mass could allow for the dark matter density to be accurately reproduced in the model.  Furthermore, we discuss the implications for the direct detection of dark matter.

We present a new approach for removing noise from images, building on the Variational Information Bottleneck. This method includes a CVF module to separate clean images from the noisy input, and a PFA module to model the underlying distribution of the clean images. By approximating the conditional probability $p(\mathcal{C}\vert \mathbf{x})$, this method uses the PFA module to refine the CVF module's predictions, thereby achieving more accurate image denoising. In addition to this, we introduce a training protocol to address the challenge of limited clean training data. Experiments show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We address the challenge of recovering a sparse signal from measurements given by $b = Ax$, with $A$ being a $m \times n$ matrix, $x$ being a $k$-sparse complex vector, and $b$ being a vector. Our primary contribution is a novel, non-constructive limit on the number of rows $m$ that the matrix $A$ must have to guarantee exact $x$ recovery using any algorithm for all possible $A$ and $x$. This bound is proportional to $k^2 \log (n/k)$. To establish this limit, we introduce a matrix property that characterizes the recovery process and demonstrate that any matrix violating this property will have a sparse code with certain desirable features. Our work offers a matrix size lower bound that improves upon a previously established lower bound of $n^{0.881}$, obtained by Grigorescu et al in 2015. Additionally, we show that the recovery process is robust to a certain level of noise in matrix $A$, specifically up to a threshold of $A$ being within a relative distance of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

This paper explores the benefits and drawbacks of using higher-order contracts
in the context of contracts and session types. Building upon the established
interleave model, the study delves into the theoretical underpinnings of
concurrent session type systems. The findings indicate that incorporating
higher-order contracts yields greater type accuracy, particularly when dealing
with combined (union) and overlapping (intersection) object types. However, the
introduction of higher-order contracts complicates the analysis of combinations
of object types. An experimental implementation in the Starling language
confirms the soundness, efficiency, and complementarity of this extension. A
specialized parser for describing higher-order contracts is developed, and this
extension is seamlessly integrated into the language with minimal added
complexity.

Our research combines the psychological theories of intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards, and demonstrates their combined impact on reinforcement learning algorithms. We discovered that incorporating both mechanisms into RL models accelerates training, improves sample efficiency and reduces the need for human interventions. A novel curiosity-driven RL approach was proposed, and its performance was evaluated on a highly complex game like Atari, where it can learn quickly from the minimal amount of human-provided rewards. We also explored various design alternatives for our approach and its effectiveness on a range of games.

We investigate how an anharmonic potential influences the motion of particles, specifically its impact on the series expansion of the oscillation frequency. Introducing a new approach based on the eigenstates of the harmonic oscillator, we can transform the problem into a problem of a particle in an anharmonic potential that is bounded by turning points. This allows us to derive a precise expression for the renormalized frequency by taking the limit of an infinite number of terms in its perturbative series. We demonstrate that this method is applicable to series expansions derived from any point in phase space and shows that the renormalized frequency depends solely on the coefficients of the expansion in terms of cosine functions, indicating a complex relationship between higher-order coefficients and the frequency. This relationship is crucial when analyzing the convergence of perturbative series. We also propose an alternative method for determining the frequency renormalization using a stochastic approach. This method is based on the principle of randomization and involves averaging over random phases drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and 2π. We show that the stochastic method is mathematically equivalent to our initial approach and provides a means to estimate the renormalized frequency from oscillations of particles with randomly chosen initial phases. We also discuss the limitations of our approach and its potential applications in analyzing anharmonic oscillations.

We've developed a broadened semiclassical approach to describe complex systems with numerous interacting loops. By incorporating the possibility of conflicting contributions from different parts of the diagram, our method achieves stable behavior in both flat and curved space settings. In our analysis, we focus on a specific theory of gravity with a broad application scope. By treating these conflicts of contributions as random variables, the theory becomes well-defined, and following standard procedures yields results consistent with previous semi-classical approaches. However, our approach provides an additional, significant benefit - it allows for the removal of infrared divergences in a natural way.

A significant concern for online platforms is the presence of rule-breakers within their user base, a challenge that poses a significant problem for Twitter, where users post millions of messages every day. In order to assess the impact of removing users who break these rules, a controlled experiment was conducted, with users who were suspended for violating rules being compared to users who were not suspended. The results of this experiment revealed that users who were suspended for violating rules were more likely to break rules at a higher rate than active users, and this rule-breaking rate continued to rise in the hours and days following their suspension, even after accounting for factors such as increased monitoring. In order to better understand this phenomenon, a model was developed that takes into account the users' past behavior, allowing for the prediction of future rule-breaking, which revealed that users who were suspended for violating rules were around 2.5 times more likely to break rules in the hours following their suspension.

The rapid advancements being driven by in-depth studies of hadron collisions at the Large Hadron Collider are also expected to lead to new opportunities for experiments at the Large Hadron Collider that combine electron-hadron and hadron-hadron collisions. This could be made possible by the development of novel accelerators that allow for simultaneous or near-simultaneous experiments with different types of beams. Three potential designs for such accelerators have been explored, taking into account the unique requirements of electron-nucleus and hadron-nucleus collisions. The proposed accelerator concepts rely on advanced technologies such as laser-electron acceleration, high-brightness ion beams, and electron beam manipulation to address these requirements independently. One possible design, the Electron-Ion Collider at the Fermilab, has been identified as particularly promising, leading to a conceptual study that will be further developed in response to the U.S. Strategy for Particle Physics Innovation Fund call.

This paper introduces an innovative ensemble method for neural networks, designed to mitigate the challenges posed by uncertain labels during training. We demonstrate that incorporating uncertainty into model aggregation significantly improves classification accuracy in uncertain labeling scenarios. To achieve this, we employ a technique of selectively eliminating network components with low confidence in their predictions, thereby promoting a diverse range of possible solutions. Ultimately, the most viable subset of network configurations is selected based on its ability to address uncertain labels.

This study develops a resource allocation strategy for V2X communications that takes into account the safety of vehicles in urban areas by creating a model representing driver behavior. The proposed approach determines the most suitable control parameters for V2X communications based on the crash risk of vehicles. A performance evaluation revealed that the strategy can effectively enhance resource allocation and reduce crash risk. The analysis showed that a higher crash risk factor allows more priority to emergency vehicles over regular vehicles, while a lower crash risk factor results in preferential treatment for regular vehicles.

The emergence of sophisticated AI-driven systems has sparked concerns over their impact on society, particularly in regards to transparency and accountability. We aim to address these concerns by investigating the potential effects of AI-powered systems on the decisions of regulators and judges, with a focus on its influence on patent infringement allegations. We introduce a novel approach to analyzing AI systems, involving a method for assessing their potential impact on the legal community. We applied our framework to a dataset of 2.5 million invalid patent claims from the USPTO, which were classified by an AI-powered system, PatScope. Our analysis revealed the AI system's performance in specific domains, enabling us to evaluate its suitability for use in different areas of patent law. We also demonstrated how the system's performance can be applied to support arguments regarding its generalizability, thereby providing valuable insights to the legal community.

This study examines the relationship between feature toggles and the rate of code integration on specific lines of code, comparing 1) the overall effectiveness of toggles, 2) their impact on software functionality, and 3) their influence on software performance. The analysis was conducted using data from 10 software projects, 7 of which utilized feature toggles. The results indicate that the presence of toggles leads to fewer code merges and improves software functionality but has no noticeable effect on performance. Additionally, feature toggues with shorter lifetimes tend to enhance functionality more than those that last longer. When comparing feature toggues by their duration, research suggests that shorter feature toggues are more often linked to increased functionality but have no significant effect on software performance. In contrast, longer feature toggues are more likely to result in fewer code merges and have no noticeable impact on functionality or performance.

Our research demonstrates the occurrence of symmetry breaking within the Navier-Stokes equations that govern incompressible fluid flow. By using a variational method and revealing the connection between a hidden symmetry and the conservation of enstrophy, we derive its time-dependent conservation at a local level. Both theoretical and numerical analyses confirm the presence of this symmetry across various flow rates, and its violation by certain disturbances results in symmetric breakdown. Our findings imply that the violation of this hidden symmetry can explain the sudden transition from laminar to turbulent fluid flow, shedding new light on this phenomenon.

This work presents the Maximum Attention visualization, a method to reveal the specific input features a deep network is concentrating on. By analyzing the largest attention weights across multiple networks, we capture the most relevant image features, even allowing for sparse support. Building upon existing techniques, our approach can be applied to any feed-forward neural network regardless of architecture. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in visualizing classification, object localization, and segmentation networks, as well as providing a direct means of understanding the semantic range of convolutional features.

We've developed a comprehensive framework for calculating the loop effects of spin-2 fields on particle interactions, relying on a simplified representation of massive graviton interactions to obtain the results. These results can be applied to various theories, such as single-field theories with additional symmetries, and specific models like the KK states in large extra dimensions, where the effects are observable. Our loop effects can be applied to the most recent analysis of dark matter scattering with nucleons by The DM-SiD collaboration to estimate uncertainty contributions. We also discuss how our findings can be applied to the search for dark matter particles with a specific mass, and explore potential constraints on new spin-2 fields using the results from direct detection experiments.

The decision of whether to pursue a military conflict or engage in negotiations with an adversary is a choice that is influenced by various factors, including the conflict's expected outcome, the costs of participating in the war or negotiation, and the risks involved. Research has shown that these costs and risks are subject to biases, with one such bias being the political bias that shapes a country's decision-making process. This study aims to analyze how political bias affects a state's expectations regarding the outcome of a war or peace negotiation and how it might lead to the escalation of conflicts. The research also explores the relationship between political bias and the occurrence of war or negotiation under specific conditions, including an adversary's strength and its own military capabilities.

A long-standing issue in cognitive neuroscience has been to understand how the brain processes sentence meaning. Specifically, researchers investigate how neural patterns related to specific word meanings, or thematic roles, overlap across different words in a sentence and across different sentences with the same word configuration. In a study examining this question, researchers conducted an ERP priming experiment where participants listened to passive sentences with the subject role, such as "the officer was shot by the perpetrator," and subsequent active sentences with the same word, such as "the perpetrator shot the victim." Results showed a significant overlap in neural patterns between the two sentence types, but only when the sentence type was consistent, indicating that the brain is actively determining the role of the word based on the sentence's context. Furthermore, this pattern of overlap was most pronounced in the anterior left temporal cortex, an area known to be involved in language processing. In contrast, other areas of the brain, such as the posterior left inferior frontal cortex, showed the opposite pattern, with the largest differences in overlap found there. Overall, these findings support the idea that the brain is not just passively retrieving pre-known word meanings, but is instead actively processing sentence meaning in a more dynamic and context-dependent way.

The detection of gravitational wave sources such as binary black hole mergers and supernovas requires precise positioning, which is essential for understanding their origins. Researchers have suggested using neutrinos as a means of pinpointing these events, but their method relies heavily on the accuracy of the neutrino angle. A recent study investigated the impact of angular accuracy on the positioning of a binary black hole trigger from LIGO/Virgo's third observing run. Results indicate that the positioning of the neutrino is highly dependent on the source's direction and the detector's location. In some cases, the predicted 3D and angular uncertainties exceed several hundred kilometers, making it challenging to confirm the binary black hole event using a neutrino. This limitation highlights the potential for multiple astrophysical neutrino sources to explain a single neutrino-GRB correlation, and the findings have significant implications for the study of neutrino astrophysics and the detection of black hole mergers.

The spatial Point Spread Function's amplitude or Strehl ratio in adaptive optics is a critical parameter that enables the determination of the primary mirror's state, including its seeing and aberrations. For systems with a dynamic measurement of the wavefront, the observed Strehl ratio is influenced by the interaction between the secondary mirror's motion, Zernike perturbations, and the control algorithm's dynamics. By examining the interaction between these factors, our analysis reveals that an accurate representation of the secondary mirror's motion is necessary to avoid misinterpreting the primary mirror's seeing and aberrations from the observed Strehl ratio. Furthermore, our work highlights the potential for using the primary mirror's spatial PSD amplitude to estimate the seeing and aberrations, even in scenarios where the wavefront is not directly measured.

This research paper examines the reliability of phonon dispersion curves for the lithium tetrachloroplatinum hexaammine compound, a potential component in nuclear medicine molecular imaging, utilizing density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory. The effectiveness of the spin-orbit coupled r2SCAN density functional in predicting phonon dispersion curves and vibrational frequencies is demonstrated, particularly in comparison to other methods such as PBE and HSE06.

We propose a hierarchical approach to computing coverability sets for coverability systems with infinite behavior. This method is applicable to very-weakly modular systems and does not rely on the systems being non-atomic. The resulting coverability sets are finite, convex, and contain the coverability sets obtained from the system's finite strongly connected components. Our approach also identifies key properties that ensure the termination of coverability set computations, which we have implemented in the tool, e.g. tool, that can be accessed at https://github.com/LSAP-Saclay/Very-WSTS-tool.

Analyzing active galactic nuclei over extended periods is a complex task due to variability caused by changes in the central region and its surroundings. To overcome this issue, our novel approach combines two techniques - active inference and time-series modeling. Active inference enables us to model the relationships between time-series data and their underlying physical meaning, whereas a non-parametric density approximation enables us to account for data that lacks a clear physical explanation. By utilizing this method, we can automatically detect and model data fluctuations without prior assumptions. Our research demonstrates the potential of this method in identifying patterns in AGN light curves and classifying them based on their spectral characteristics. Future research will focus on applying this method to a large dataset, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of AGN variability patterns.

Building upon the foundation laid by Schr\"odinger, Everett, and DeWitt, the quantum theory of reality posits that every time a quantum measurement occurs, the state of the universe expands, creating numerous branches, each containing only a subset of the initial universe. This branching results in a multitude of parallel universes, each differing from the others due to variations in density matrices at specific points. This expansion of the quantum state raises questions about the emergence of objective reality and the nature of branching. This is addressed by Quantum Darwinism, a theory that explains how the environment's many-body degrees of freedom collect and disseminate objective information about the branches of the quantum state. This process is crucial for the emergence of objective reality and is demonstrated in this article using the example of a simple harmonic oscillator. In this example, the information is stored in the vibrational modes of the environment's collective degrees of freedom, and are subsequently used to determine which branch of the quantum state is the correct one. This is done by using the information to break ties between branches, and are used to determine which branch of the quantum state is the correct one. This process is also used to demonstrate how information is collected and disseminated in the example of an experiment with an atom and are used to determine the existence of objective reality.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to estimating the reachable state space of discrete-time dynamical systems with uncertain input variables. The proposed technique refines an initial over-approximation of the reachable state space through iterative calculations, using the convex body defined by the over-approximation and its normal vectors. The method involves calculating the preimages of this convex body, projecting them onto the current state space, and then generating tighter bounds of the reachable state space using these projected images. The tighter bounds are computed using second-order representations of system dynamics combined with sum-of-squares programming and convex optimization techniques. The proposed method is demonstrated through a simulation study of a vehicle navigating a road network.

Deep learning models trained with sparse gradient backpropagation have shown significant success in solving machine learning problems that involve tabular data. Nevertheless, the process of finding the optimal hyperparameters for these models is challenging due to their high computational requirements and the poor performance observed in some models. In an effort to address these issues, a new model called SAINT has been developed, combining a novel transformation to reduce the computational costs of sparse gradient updates with a self-regulating mechanism that prevents overfitting. SAINT's results on real-world datasets significantly outperform other leading techniques, including random forests, and demonstrates superior performance with substantial improvements of over 50% when compared to the traditional deep neural network models on specific problems. SAINT's performance has also shown significant enhancements in the presence of missing data, outperforming other leading techniques by substantial margins of over 50% on datasets with missing values.

The effectiveness of transfer learning (TL) heavily relies on the similarity between the training and testing environments. TL methods, however, often struggle when the domains are highly dissimilar due to differences in features, sample distributions, and classification targets. This study focuses on adapting TL for environments where the domains are distinct but the underlying feature structures are similar. We introduce a model called NetDropout that leverages random dropout layers in both domains to create diverse feature representations during training, thereby promoting similarity in feature structures. We also propose an evaluation metric to measure domain similarity based on the model's performance. Experiments conducted on multiple imbalanced classification tasks within the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate the model's superior performance compared to other TL methods.

In quantum chromodynamics, the interaction of particles leads to a breakdown in symmetry with the emergence of hadrons, a phenomenon known as hadronization. By examining the correlation between color and flavor, researchers can study this process. A key aspect of this process involves the fluctuations in a quantity known as the 'colour charge operator', the magnitude of which indicates the strength of symmetry breaking. Previous calculations have shown that these fluctuations increase as certain momentum thresholds are reached, at which point the particles begin to interact strongly. This interaction leads to a breakdown in the symmetry of space-time. The fluctuations in this quantity are measured at different momentum levels and show a significant change at the same point at which strong interaction begins. This study provides a more detailed analysis of this process by comparing its various components. It shows that this change in symmetry is due to a combination of factors including strong interaction and the way matter is arranged. The findings of this study are relevant to a range of research areas including the study of light and heavy particles, the way that particles arrange themselves, and the study of particles moving through matter.

This research paper details our initial attempt to detect dark matter particles through a specific process using the LHCb detector at the 13 TeV LHC energy level. We analyzed data collected from 2015 to 2018, with a total volume of 14.7 inverse femtobarns. We narrowed our focus to a specific dark matter-dominant scenario, where the particles in question break down into a pair of bottom quarks via a heavy, complex particle. Our investigation revealed no signs of this hypothetical dark matter particle. As a result, we established a limitation that the interaction between the dark matter particle and standard model particles is below 1.16 x 10^-3 pb at a mass of 100 GeV, with a 95% degree of certainty.

Researchers have long sought to improve the process of locating software concepts. A significant development in this area has been achieved through a crowdsourcing approach, where online communities share knowledge in large volumes. This knowledge can be utilized to create more effective concept localization techniques, but existing methods require a considerable investment of time for training, rendering them unsuitable for practical use. This paper presents a novel machine learning technique that utilizes crowdsourced knowledge to locate software concepts, demonstrating its potential through a real-world application in a Java repository. The proposed method, SOCO, surpasses existing approaches in concept localization, offering a more practical solution that does not require extensive pre-training and can be easily integrated into widely-used software mining tools.

This paper examines the preconditioning issue for the matrix derived from the Stokes system, and develops a block-diagonal preconditioner that demonstrates superior convergence for GMRES iteration. The proposed preconditioner is particularly useful in large-scale Stokes system simulations. An analysis based on the traditional idea is also provided to explain the effectiveness of the preconditioner, and it is further supported by numerical examples that validate the theoretical analysis.

In abstractive dialogue summarization, a key challenge is identifying and inferring crucial dialogue elements that bear significant weights and should be included in summaries. To address this, a novel approach is proposed that leverages discourse relations for abstractive dialogue summarization. This approach involves training two neural models: one for extracting important dialogue elements and assigning weights, and another for summarizing with the generated discourse relations as inputs. Our experiments on two datasets reveal that the proposed method surpasses previous benchmarks, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance.

This study explores the potential of deep learning to simplify the complex problem of Doppler broadening in cross-section applications. Traditional methods for simulating Doppler effects are computationally expensive and often lead to inaccurate results. By leveraging deep learning techniques, researchers can efficiently calculate the Doppler broadening of cross-sections across various energy and velocity distributions. A novel deep learning model was developed, incorporating multiple architectures to account for interactions between neutrons and fission products. Through extensive training on a comprehensive dataset, the model achieved accurate results, demonstrating its ability to generalize to unseen data. Notably, the proposed approach outperformed traditional approximations, offering significant potential for applications in reactor design and operational efficiency.

Given that $n$-pre-Lie algebras have already been studied, it is natural to investigate higher-order versions, specifically the $(n + 1)$-pre-Lie algebras, which build upon the given $n$-pre-Lie algebras, and in this context, a method to explore multi-branded filtrations of $(n + 1)$-pre-Lie algebras is addressed, leading to the development of a cohomology theory that enables the classification of $(n + 1)$-pre-Lie algebra extensions and provides conditions for the realization of extended structures, and further applications to the realm of super $n$-pre-Lie algebras are also investigated.

This research presents an advanced non-orthogonal multiple access scheme incorporating simultaneous wireless charging for massive MIMO systems.
