The task of classifying distorted crystal structures from experimental X-ray data, affected by thermal vibrations, is complicated by noisy patterns in the 3D Fourier maps derived from these data. We developed an effective denoising technique, utilizing real-space electron density maps refined through simulated experimental conditions. This method, applied to over 1000 crystal structures (approximately 100 unique structures) with diverse distortions, resulted in substantial improvements in classification accuracy. Specifically, our approach achieved classification rates exceeding 90% on over 90% of the structures, which is comparable to the accuracy achieved with undistorted data. This technique also enables the extraction of meaningful electron density maps, retaining significant amounts of structural information despite the distortions. We also found that our denoising method, when applied to the Fourier maps, can enhance classification accuracy. This work presents a novel approach for post-experiment data processing and highlights its potential in extracting valuable structural information from noisy experimental data.

A novel approach is presented for determining water properties and transport dynamics within a marine environment, utilizing a combination of an Eulerian grid and a Lagrangian particle method to track idealised water particles. By integrating Eulerian and Lagrangian analysis methods, a unified framework for quantifying mixing and transport has been achieved from both time-independent and time-dependent perspectives. Eulerian analysis is applied to a fixed grid, while the Lagrangian method tracks idealised water particles. Water characteristics are divided into three categories: the Eulerian mean, Lagrangian mean, and ensemble mean, which serve as indicators for specific aspects of the environment. Eulerian analysis is ideal for quantifying stationary water properties, while Lagrangian analysis is more suitable for dynamic water properties. Ensemble mean values represent the overall water properties across the domain at a particular time.

The Murnaghan equation of state (EOS) is widely applied to solids, but its application to hydrocarbons has faced challenges due to its inability to effectively account for the complex interactions between molecules.  Despite this limitation, the Murnaghan EOS can still be used to quantify the inherent disorder in molecular hydrocarbons.  By treating the Murnaghan EOS as an indicator of anisotropic behavior, researchers have used the anharmonicity parameter (γ) to quantify the disorder in these systems and have found a correlation between γ and the number of rotatable bonds.  Interestingly, the anharmonicity parameter can provide a molecular basis for the increased NBO in these systems, suggesting that the underlying cause of this phenomenon is the disorder in the molecular structure rather than differences in bonding patterns.

This paper examines the semi-discrete damped modified Camassa-Holm equation, 
which is a discrete analogue of a significant integrable system in the field of soliton solutions. 
By employing non-local conservation laws, our analysis confirms that the discrete equation retains 
an hydrodynamic reduction under a continuum limit and reveals that it retains an integrable form, 
specifically a 3 by 3 Lax pair, which simplifies into a 2 by 2 matrix form. This work further 
establishes that the discrete equation possesses a bi-Hamiltonian formulation and a 
compatible Bäcklund transformation by employing a Lagrangian, defining Adams-Bashforth time-discretization, 
and identifying a suitable discrete variational derivative. Consequently, properties such as 
Lax triad, bi-Hamiltonian structure, and Bäcklund transformations are proven to be invariant 
when the discrete equation undergoes a continuous limit.

In recent years, a physical interpretation of the quantum world has gained significant attention, particularly one proposed by Bozzi and Ghiani, which views particles as inherent degrees of freedom, existing independently within quantum theory. This framework, building on de Broglie-Boell's theory and Verma's proposal, offers a new perspective on the nature of reality. This research aims to explore how the statistical principles of Bohmian mechanics can be applied within the context of a free particle moving in a deterministic manner, as described by the de Broglian solution to the Newton equation. This approach will be used to define probability distributions for position, momentum, and other related variables, enabling the derivation of a momentum distribution consistent with the de Broglian solution. This work will contribute to a comprehensive understanding of a statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics, particularly one that aligns with the de Broglian solution.

We have conducted an in-depth study on compact binaries consisting of equal-mass components, with one being a black hole and the other a boson star. We focused on a specific type of binary where the boson star's mass is nearly equal to its black hole counterpart's mass, allowing us to accurately model the boson star using Schwarzschild coordinates. We analyzed the binary's dynamics, finding that the boson star's response to curvature-induced potential differs significantly from the black hole's behavior, leading to distinct spin and scalar charges for the two components. We observed that the binary's energy and energy dissipation are influenced by these differences, particularly when the black hole's spin is higher than a specific threshold. Our results show that the black hole-boson star binary exhibits unique features not seen in black hole-neutron star binaries, potentially opening up new avenues for exploring astrophysical phenomena.

The YOLO model, known for its real-time object detection, processes input images through a series of convolutional neural network layers. In contrast to other models, which use separate layers to generate region proposals and process features, YOLO integrates proposal generation and feature processing within a single network architecture. This integration allows for a direct correlation between input images and fixed region proposals across multiple layers, resulting in a significant amount of redundant information. A notable aspect of YOLO is that earlier layers, which are responsible for processing smaller region proposals, and later layers, which are responsible for processing larger region proposals, both contribute to the final output. However, the repetition of information leads to redundancy, and the existing backpropagation algorithms do not account for this phenomenon. As a result, the impact of redundant information on the performance of YOLO is not adequately addressed. This paper proposes a novel algorithm, referred to as Knowledge Distillation with Pruning (KDPr), which eliminates redundant information within YOLO. KDPr is based on the principle that earlier layers, which are responsible for processing smaller region proposals, and later layers, which are responsible for processing larger region proposals, should not both contribute to the final output. This research explores and quantifies the manner in which prominent business leaders communicate during a financial upheaval. We establish a framework for analyzing how these leaders use language when speaking about the crisis and the economy. We employ human and algorithmic evaluators, as well as a hybrid assessment method to train and tune our system. We discover that our model surpasses random predictions in this task. Furthermore, our study reveals that analyzing quotes from business figures can provide valuable insights into market communication patterns and facilitate a deeper understanding of these leaders' behavior.

One of the most effective data exploration, summarization, and knowledge-discovery tools is the concept lattice, derived from power sets of attributes and their combinations. Various applications, such as enhancing prediction capabilities, have been found to leverage concept lattice elements, especially through set-valued attributes and concept learning. This paper introduces a novel, fully-supervised deep learning architecture, built upon the concept lattice, to boost classification and regression performance. This approach involves encoding each training sample into its corresponding concept lattice node, using set-valued attributes, and employing transfer learning to derive weights from pre-trained nodes. Experimental results on multiple synthetic datasets and real-world applications indicate that this architecture surpasses current deep learning models, especially when dealing with full samples in each epoch, producing an average improvement of 4.2% and reaching an accuracy of 100% in certain cases.

The normative implications of machine learning evaluations are often influenced by unexamined assumptions. These assumptions can be found in the criteria used to evaluate model performance. We argue that it is crucial to identify and justify these criteria. If not, they may reflect the biases and beliefs of experts in the field, researchers, or those who fund their work. These unexamined assumptions can result in machine learning evaluations that are ethically problematic. For instance, using parametric statistical tests to evaluate multiple parametric hypothesis tests can lead to the perpetuation of gender biases, as it requires similar data distributions across different groups. Similarly, requiring high levels of precision in model predictions can be at odds with certain ethical principles. We illustrate these issues with practical examples and demonstrate how these assumptions can be made more explicit, thereby mitigating the negative effects on social norms.

The RaRecognize framework is a fair classification method that provides two output values - a prediction and a score, which determines the confidence level of the majority and minority classes within a dataset. By doing so, it ensures fairness by accounting for the differences in model performance between the two groups. Unlike other methods, RaRecognize achieves fairness without compromising accuracy, thus outputting the true classification results. The proposed approach is supported by experiments on real-world classification datasets.

In scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), ptychography is a powerful imaging tool, yet it can be hindered by several limitations. We examine the impact of two significant factors: the limited sample size accessible to the electron beam, and the unfocused electron wave used for scanning. We have now developed a self-consistent ptychographic method that effectively compensates for the unfocused electron wave, which significantly enhances image clarity. We demonstrate this improvement using simulated images of various nanostructures and high-quality experimental data from a perovskite oxide sample, achieving detailed resolution of 0.85 Angstroms.

We introduce a novel method for calculating long-term averages and correlation values in Markovian models based on their underlying algebra and topology, which are determined by their state space configuration. By utilizing the concept of a random process as a morphism, we establish a parallel transfer within the category of these configurations, ultimately deriving key equations from the algebraic structure of our target configurations. By leveraging the properties of this structure, we derive an explicit formula for calculating long-term averages and correlation values, which is demonstrated across various model scenarios. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between our method and the Lagrangian formalism in physical systems, showing that our calculated averages and correlation values align with those obtained through this traditional approach.

Over the past ten years, the concept of reservoir computing has been explored thoroughly, prompting a comprehensive review of the literature to date. Focus is placed on how the characteristics of the input signals affect the efficacy of reservoir computing, particularly through an in-depth examination of past reviews on this subject. In addition, the discussion encompasses various real-world applications of reservoir computing, such as how individual components of the model are assigned credit, and future directions for research within this domain.

We investigate the spatial arrangement and quantum interactions within a system of three identical bosons confined under a harmonic trap by solving the three-body Schrödinger equation. We represent the system's wave function in a basis of three-body configurations, which allows us to analyze the effects of two-body and three-body interactions on the system. We find that increasing interactions cause the separation of particles, aligning with the predictions of mean-field theories at high interaction strengths. Interestingly, our results indicate that the particle separation transitions from a regime of weak interactions to one of strong interactions at a critical point corresponding to a dimer formation, with significant implications for the study of interacting Bose systems.

A novel method utilizes time-encodable photons to assess quantum kernels, effectively turning complex quantum computation tasks into a format amenable to single-photon detectors capable of time-resolving technology. Leveraging the temporal encoding of photons, this approach efficiently determines the values of quantum kernels within single-excitation subspaces, with potential for adaptation into a broader framework for evaluating arbitrary-time Markovian processes. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of this method through its application to modeling the dynamics of spin systems, where we showcase its ability to approximate the time-evolved quantum kernel and illustrate its potential for quantum machine learning tasks via supervised learning. Ultimately, this approach is found to be highly promising for marking the beginning of a new era in the foundations of quantum computing.

The performance of a 2-D monomial polynomial basis in function approximation is evaluated. On a mesh-based domain, the approximation quality on a given element is significantly influenced by the size of the element and the degree of the polynomial basis. As a result, a high-order 2-D monomial polynomial basis is proposed in this paper to address the local imbalance issue. By selectively increasing the polynomial degrees based on the element size, the high-order basis can achieve an average error rate that is at least as good as a standard high-order polynomial basis. Experiments conducted on various computational models demonstrate the potential of the proposed basis for enhancing numerical methods on unstructured meshes.
